body_text: When BILL, Zoho Books, and FreshBooks Stop Working Key Takeaways BILL.com’s cash application breaks down when customers bundle multiple invoices into one ACH transfer or use unrecognized reference numbers. Zoho Books offers a free plan for businesses under $50,000 annual revenue but lacks multi-currency support and collection efficiency metrics. Automated cash application, matching bank deposits to invoices, separates tools built for one-off billing from those handling recurring revenue. SaaS firms with high-volume subscription renewals often outgrow BILL.com once payment volumes exceed a few hundred transactions per month. BILL.com started as an accounts payable platform and excels at vendor bill pay, but its AR features rely on exact invoice number matching. Zoho Books’ reporting layer doesn’t surface aging receivables or collection metrics finance teams need once revenue crosses seven figures. Most integrated invoice-to-cash platforms handle invoice creation and payment collection well but struggle with automated deposit reconciliation at scale. Quick Comparison Summary An invoice goes out. The customer pays. The payment lands in your bank. Your system matches that deposit to the right invoice. Most platforms handle the first two steps. The third step, automated cash application, is where things fall apart once you’re running recurring revenue. What Sets These Tools Apart BILL.com started as an AP automation platform and later added AR features. It excels at vendor bill pay and approval workflows, but its cash application relies on exact invoice number matching. A customer pays multiple invoices in one ACH transfer? Uses a reference number you don’t recognize? You’re back to manual reconciliation. The platform manages finances for thousands of mid-market companies, but SaaS firms with high-volume subscription renewals often hit a ceiling when payment volumes scale beyond a few hundred transactions per month. Zoho Books offers a free plan for businesses under $50,000 in annual revenue. It includes invoicing, expense tracking, and bank reconciliation. Where it falters: multi-currency support remains limited, and the reporting layer doesn’t surface aging receivables or collection efficiency metrics finance teams need once revenue crosses seven figures. One user on G2 described setting up workflows that handle invoice creation to payment reminders without manual input, which works for service businesses with predictable monthly billing. Subscription companies with usage-based pricing or mid-cycle plan changes see more friction. FreshBooks supports only 7 out of 32 tax compliance features, a 14.52% score compared to the market average of 46.18%. That gap matters less for domestic service firms than for SaaS companies operating across state or national tax jurisdictions. The platform focuses on invoicing and payment collection, which keeps the interface clean but leaves finance teams building spreadsheets to track dunning effectiveness, payment retry success rates, or churn tied to failed billing. QuickBooks Online , by comparison, manages finances for over 7 million businesses and pays over 18 million U.S. workers through its payroll arm, offering deeper financial control and automation depth. Pricing and What You Actually Pay Wave keeps entry costs low with a free plan and paid features starting at $19 per month. QuickBooks Online runs promotional pricing as low as $2.22 per month for the first six months, then scales from $20 to $275 monthly depending on the plan. Zoho Books starts at $20 per month for paid tiers, topping out at $70. FreshBooks and BILL.com both sit in the $20 to $200 range depending on user count and feature access. The real cost shows up after you send the invoice. If your payment processor deposits funds daily but your accounting system requires manual matching, you’re paying an AR specialist to reconcile transactions that should run automatically. For teams processing fewer than 50 invoices per month, that overhead stays manageable. Once you cross 200 monthly transactions, common for SaaS firms with annual and monthly billing mixed together, manual cash application becomes a bottleneck that delays revenue recognition and clouds your cash position. Teams outgrow these platforms when subscription revenue becomes the majority of their income and payment matching stops being a one-to-one problem. If your invoices reference plan IDs, usage tiers, or proration logic, the cash application engine needs to parse more than an invoice number. That’s where general-purpose accounting tools start requiring workarounds. Why You’d Consider Alternatives Evaluating alternative platforms typically comes down to one operational question: what happens after the payment arrives? For businesses running subscriptions or recurring invoices, the answer determines whether you can scale your accounts receivable or remain stuck manually reconciling deposits every week. When Payment Matching Becomes the Bottleneck The evaluation becomes urgent when the gap between bank deposits and ledger entries widens. Standard platforms assume a simple one-to-one relationship between an invoice and a payment. Any deviation from this pattern disrupts the sync. When customers pay out of sequence or use non-standard payment methods, the automated flow halts, forcing your team to manually verify each transaction against open balances. The gap shows up most clearly in subscription models where billing cycles are continuous. Customers may pay early, late, or combine multiple outstanding balances into a single transfer. Even robust general ledger systems struggle with these variations, logging the total deposit but requiring manual intervention to distribute the funds across the correct line items. Service businesses with retainers, agencies billing milestone-based projects, and consultancies managing recurring clients see this pattern repeat. The invoice goes out cleanly. The payment arrives on time. Then the finance team opens a spreadsheet to figure out what it covers. Selection Factors That Matter for Recurring Revenue Automated bank reconciliation separates tools built for one-off invoices from those designed for recurring billing. Look for platforms that match payments to invoices and streamline cash application without manual work. When a customer sends a single wire transfer to cover a monthly subscription, an overdue balance, and a one-time service fee, a specialized system parses the metadata to update all three records simultaneously, rather than flagging the transaction as an exception. User access limits become a constraint faster than expected. Xero allows unlimited users on all plans, which matters when your billing team grows or when project managers need read-only access to invoice status. Zoho Books caps users by plan tier, and FreshBooks charges per additional seat. As teams scale from five to fifteen people, per-seat pricing can shift total cost of ownership by 40-60% compared to unlimited-user models. Workflow automation depth determines whether invoice-to-cash runs on autopilot or requires constant manual intervention. Standard platforms can automate outbound reminders and invoice generation, but they often stop short of closing the loop when the payment returns. Feature BILL Zoho Books FreshBooks Blixo Cash application automation Invoice number matching only Basic allocation Invoice number matching only AI-powered matching User limits Tiered by plan Tiered by plan Per-seat pricing 3 (Team), 5 (Business), custom (Enterprise) Recurring billing Supported Supported Supported Built for subscriptions Multi-invoice payments Manual reconciliation Manual reconciliation Manual reconciliation Automated allocation Common Needs That Push Teams to Reevaluate You’ll hit the ceiling when your accounting team starts treating the platform as a database instead of a workflow engine. That looks like exporting transaction lists to Excel, manually tagging payments by customer, or building side systems to track which deposits cover which invoices. These workarounds signal that the tool handles data storage but not business logic. International operations expose another constraint. Businesses managing cross-border payments need platforms that handle multi-currency reconciliation without manual exchange rate adjustments. Oracle NetSuite handles complex international operations starting at $99 per user per month plus licensing fees, but that infrastructure is overkill for a 20-person agency. The gap between FreshBooks and NetSuite leaves most recurring-revenue businesses either underserved or overpaying. Blixo’s intelligent matching engine automates the step where BILL, Zoho Books, and FreshBooks treat recurring revenue like one-off transactions. The platform applies payments automatically, eliminating the manual reconciliation work that bogs down finance teams managing subscriptions and recurring invoices. Feature Comparison When you’re evaluating integrated invoice-to-cash applications, most comparison charts focus on the features everyone already checks: invoicing templates, payment gateway integrations, expense tracking. The real differentiator shows up after a customer pays, specifically, how each platform handles cash application when deposits don’t arrive with perfect invoice references. Businesses hit the reconciliation wall around the same point: when monthly recurring revenue crosses six figures or when payment volumes outpace the capacity of manual ledger updates. At that threshold, standard invoicing tools begin forcing administrative overhead back into your daily operations. Payment Matching and Reconciliation Depth BILL.com routes payments well but operates on an architecture designed primarily for accounts payable. The system’s underlying logic expects a clean, one-to-one match for incoming funds. When a customer uses their own purchase order reference or combines multiple balances, the system struggles to allocate the deposit, requiring manual intervention to reconcile the ledger. FreshBooks handles basic invoicing efficiently, but it lacks the automation depth needed for recurring billing. One industry observer noted that it “can’t match” the financial control larger businesses require once invoice volume scales. The platform’s simplified tax structure requires manual adjustments for complex regional rules, and its per-seat pricing model adds overhead as you expand your administrative team. Zoho Books provides a solid foundation for straightforward billing cycles. The challenge surfaces when managing cross-border transactions or complex reporting requirements. Users frequently note that the platform lacks the depth required for complex reconciliation scenarios, particularly when payments arrive through third-party processors that deduct fees before deposit, leaving partial amounts that must be matched manually. Xero emphasizes bank feed integration and real-time reconciliation suggestions, which speeds up matching when transactions are simple. The system flags likely matches based on amount and date, but it struggles with the same bundled-payment scenarios that trip up other platforms. When a customer consolidates invoices from different billing periods into a single transfer, Xero’s suggestions become less reliable, and you’re back to manual review. When Feature Gaps Force Workarounds QuickBooks Online serves as a comprehensive financial hub, offering capabilities across payroll, inventory, and project tracking. However, its breadth doesn’t always translate to depth in cash application. When a business receives a consolidated ACH transfer covering several billing periods, the system still requires manual allocation across individual invoice records, limiting its utility for high-volume subscription models. Blixo is built around the specific pain point that surfaces in subscription billing: payment arrives, it’s the right amount, but your system can’t automatically figure out which invoices it covers because the customer didn’t include your invoice numbers in the wire reference. That’s where fuzzy matching and AI-assisted reconciliation shift the workload from your finance team back to the software. The manual matching work that used to occupy Monday mornings turns into a quick review and approval workflow. Oracle NetSuite sits at the enterprise end, designed for complex business structures and multi-entity operations. It’s built for mid-market companies with international subsidiaries, dedicated accounting teams, and the need for advanced revenue recognition rules. The decision isn’t whether NetSuite has more features, it’s whether you need the features it offers over simpler alternatives. Automation That Matches Your Billing Model Envoice focuses on AI-driven expense management at accessible entry pricing, while other budget-conscious options deliver strong value at their price points. Neither was designed for recurring revenue reconciliation. They handle invoicing well. They don’t handle the cash application bottleneck that emerges when you’re managing dozens of active subscriptions and customers pay through bank transfers instead of credit cards. The shift from affordability to feature gaps happens quietly. You start with a low-cost tool, invoice your first group of customers without friction, then hit month six and realize you’re spending hours each week reconciling payments manually. That’s when advanced cash application stops being a nice-to-have and becomes the feature you should have evaluated from the start. The difference between platforms becomes visible not in their marketing pages but in how much time your finance lead spends each week fixing what should have been automated. Performance Comparison The difference between platforms built for one-time invoicing and those designed for recurring revenue shows up clearest when cash hits your bank account in ways your system didn’t anticipate. A customer pays three months at once. Another splits a yearly invoice across two ACH transfers. A third uses their own purchase order number as the payment reference. The platform that handles these scenarios automatically scales with your business instead of consuming your finance team’s calendar. Processing Speed Under Recurring Billing Load Major general-ledger platforms offer infrastructure capable of handling massive transaction volumes, but their scale advantage is optimized for standard batch processing rather than complex matching. When a customer consolidates multiple subscription payments under a custom reference code, the bottleneck is not system throughput, it is the underlying cash application logic that determines whether your team must manually reconcile the deposit. FreshBooks scales well for project-based billing where each invoice is a discrete event. One G2 reviewer noted that its time tracking and expense workflows handle hundreds of client projects without slowdown. The performance gap shows up when you shift from project invoicing to subscription billing: a creative agency with 50 clients sending one invoice per project each month sees fast reconciliation, but a SaaS company with 50 customers on monthly auto-renew hits manual reconciliation on every customer who updates their payment method or pays multiple months at once. Xero processes invoices quickly and supports collaborative workflows as your finance team expands. Raw transaction speed doesn’t reduce reconciliation hours when payments deviate from expected patterns. A batch of invoices might clear in seconds, yet if customers bundle payments or use custom reference codes, your team must still manually resolve those exceptions. Resource Costs at Scale The shift from one-time invoicing to recurring billing changes what “resource usage” means. It’s no longer about storage for invoice PDFs or API rate limits for payment gateway calls. The real resource drain is human time spent on reconciliation exceptions. Growing companies hit an inflection point where their accounts receivable clerk goes from part-time to full-time because deposit matching became a manual job. Three cost categories matter when evaluating performance at scale: Manual reconciliation hours compound faster than revenue. A business at $75K MRR with 150 active subscriptions typically sees 10-15 reconciliation exceptions per week when using standard invoicing tools. That’s four to six hours of controller time. Triple the customer base to 450 subscriptions, and exception volume doesn’t triple, it quadruples or quintuples, because payment behavior becomes less predictable as your mix of customer types expands. Failed payment retry logic creates a secondary performance tax. Zoho Books and FreshBooks both handle dunning emails, but neither automates the cash application step after a retry succeeds. When a subscription payment fails on the 1st, retries on the 5th, and clears on the 8th, you’re manually matching that deposit to an invoice that’s now a week old with a reference number the bank generated, not the one your system expected. Integration overhead scales non-linearly. Connecting Stripe or Braintree to your accounting platform works smoothly until you need to reconcile platform fees, refunds, and partial captures in the same deposit batch. QuickBooks Online offers next-level financial control according to users who’ve migrated from simpler tools, but that control still assumes payments arrive as discrete, labeled transactions rather than as bundled settlement files. Xero’s bank feed reconciliation handles high transaction volumes efficiently, but when payment processors batch-settle transactions, the platform still requires manual intervention to split a single deposit line into its component invoices. One finance director reported spending 90 minutes each week unwinding Stripe settlement batches that included 30-40 individual subscription payments, even though Xero’s raw processing speed was never the constraint. The performance gap that matters most isn’t listed in any speed benchmarks. It’s the difference between a system that handles 95% of deposits automatically and one that handles 60%, because that 35-point gap translates directly to whether your finance team scales with revenue or becomes the constraint on growth. Pros and Cons Every integrated invoice-to-cash application looks capable on paper. The limitations only surface after you’ve onboarded your team, migrated your customer list, and started processing payments at scale. The same friction points emerge across BILL, Zoho Books, and FreshBooks once businesses cross the threshold where manual oversight of accounts receivable becomes a daily administrative burden. Where BILL.com Excels and Where It Struggles BILL.com handles vendor bill pay better than most alternatives. If your workflow involves approval routing for outgoing payments, BILL’s strength is in AP automation, making it a strong choice for businesses that prioritize outbound payment workflows. The weakness shows up in cash application. The system expects exact invoice number references. Any deviation requires manual intervention. When a customer pays multiple balances at once or uses an unrecognized reference code, the automated reconciliation fails. This is manageable for businesses sending occasional project invoices. It becomes a bottleneck for SaaS companies processing high-volume recurring billing cycles. The platform also struggles with multi-entity accounting. If you’re running separate legal entities or managing client trust accounts, BILL’s architecture forces you into separate logins and manual consolidation. QuickBooks Online handles multiple entities within a single workspace, which matters when you’re preparing consolidated reports. Zoho Books: Free Until It Isn’t Zoho Books offers a free plan for early-stage companies under the $50,000 annual revenue threshold, making it an accessible starting point. Its basic automation handles standard invoice generation, and its multi-currency support covers fundamental international billing needs like EUR and GBP invoicing. The platform hits its ceiling when you need advanced reporting or deeper tax compliance. If you’re invoicing across multiple jurisdictions or dealing with complex VAT regulations, the lack of built-in compliance features means you’ll spend time exporting data to spreadsheets to generate the reports your accountant needs. User access is another constraint. Zoho Books charges per additional user, a pricing model that works for solo consultants but becomes expensive as your team expands. By the time you add a third or fourth team member, the per-seat costs can significantly increase your monthly software spend compared to platforms with flat-rate pricing. FreshBooks: Built for Simplicity, Not Scale FreshBooks wins on ease of setup. You can start invoicing within minutes, and the interface assumes zero accounting knowledge. That simplicity is deliberate, FreshBooks targets freelancers and small service businesses that need basic invoicing without the complexity of double-entry bookkeeping. The tradeoff is depth. FreshBooks lacks the workflow automation and ledger depth that subscription businesses need once they begin processing dozens of recurring invoices monthly. The platform is optimized for simple, single-payment transactions. It does not support automated matching for consolidated deposits, and its reporting remains too surface-level to track complex subscription metrics across multiple payment processors. Tax compliance is another gap. FreshBooks covers basic sales tax calculation but lacks the depth for cross-border invoicing under VAT or GST regimes. If your customer base spans multiple countries, you’ll need to verify tax treatment manually or export to a more capable system. Companies with even modest international revenue, say 30% of transactions outside their home country, quickly outpace what FreshBooks can validate automatically. The Real Deciding Factor The decision point has shifted to what happens after adoption. All three platforms handle basic invoicing well. The differences emerge in payment reconciliation depth, user access constraints, and compliance coverage. As transaction volumes grow, the cumulative administrative burden of manual reconciliation scales rapidly, turning what should be automated tasks into a significant weekly time sink. Businesses outgrow FreshBooks first, usually within six months of launching a subscription product. Zoho Books lasts longer but hits reporting and compliance limits around the $150K revenue mark. BILL.com works for companies with heavy AP workflows but forces manual reconciliation on the AR side unless every customer pays with perfect invoice references, which in practice means almost no one. The gap widens as transaction volume increases: at 500 monthly payments, the time difference between automated matching and manual reconciliation represents nearly a full-time employee. Use Cases and Ideal Users Integrated invoice-to-cash applications split cleanly along one fault line: how they handle the week after your customer pays. If your business sends one-off project invoices to a handful of clients, standard tools will suffice. The friction surfaces when your billing model shifts to recurring subscriptions, where the cash application bottleneck becomes the primary operational constraint. When BILL.com Fits Your Workflow BILL.com handles vendor bill pay and approval routing better than most alternatives. If your AP team processes hundreds of outgoing payments each month and needs multi-level sign-off workflows, BILL’s core strength shows up in those outbound transactions. The platform works well for businesses where accounts payable volume exceeds accounts receivable complexity. The weakness emerges in recurring billing reconciliation. When incoming deposits don’t map cleanly to individual invoices, the automated flow halts. One G2 reviewer noted this friction: while the system handles outbound vendor payments smoothly, managing incoming subscription deposits requires significant manual oversight to ensure payments are applied to the correct customer accounts. Choose BILL when your primary pain point is managing vendor relationships and approval workflows, not when you’re scaling subscription renewals. The platform processes over 180 million transactions annually across its user base, but that volume tilts heavily toward outbound vendor payments rather than inbound subscription cash application. Where FreshBooks and Zoho Books Hit Their Ceiling FreshBooks focuses on invoicing and payment collection, it’s built for service businesses sending project-based invoices, not for recurring billing at scale. The platform serves over 30 million users globally, but that adoption concentrates in freelance and agency workflows where each invoice represents discrete project work. When your revenue model shifts to subscriptions, the invoice-centric architecture starts creating friction rather than reducing it. Zoho Books automates VAT and GST calculations for regional requirements and integrates with 180+ Zoho applications, making it a natural fit if you’re already embedded in the Zoho ecosystem. When deposits arrive without standard references, the reconciliation work shifts back to your finance team. Users report spending 3-4 hours per week on manual cash application once they reach consistent subscription renewal volumes, highlighting the limits of its standard matching engine. Skip both platforms once you’re processing recurring subscription renewals that customers pay in bundled deposits. The tools assume each payment maps to a single invoice. That assumption breaks down as your customer base grows and payment patterns become less predictable. The Recurring Revenue Reconciliation Test You’ll know it’s time to evaluate alternatives when your finance team starts dedicating Monday mornings to matching bank deposits against open invoices. Even with robust general ledger platforms, the system struggles when customers bundle payments. The constraint isn’t processing speed, it’s the cash application logic that assumes a simple one-to-one relationship between deposits and invoices. Businesses adopt these platforms for invoicing and payment collection, then hit the reconciliation wall once recurring revenue scales. The tools work well until payment matching becomes the bottleneck. At that threshold, you need integrated invoice-to-cash applications designed for subscription billing, not project-based invoicing retrofitted with recurring invoice templates. Finance teams report that manual cash application errors increase by 23% when processing bundled subscription payments compared to single-invoice deposits, creating downstream revenue recognition issues that compound over quarters. What to Actually Do The decision between integrated invoice-to-cash applications comes down to one constraint: how much manual reconciliation you’re willing to absorb once monthly recurring revenue scales. Standard tools handle invoice generation and payment collection well enough. The bottleneck surfaces when payment matching fails to scale, forcing your team to spend valuable time on administrative tasks instead of strategic growth. When Each Option Makes Sense BILL.com fits workflows where approval routing matters more than AR automation. If your finance team processes hundreds of outgoing payments each month and needs multi-level approval workflows, BILL’s AP strength justifies the manual reconciliation work on the receivables side. If your business runs on subscriptions, the lack of automated AR matching will eventually create a scaling bottleneck. Zoho Books works when you need regional tax automation built into the platform rather than bolted on through integrations. The mobile app earned a 4.3 rating from 8,200 reviews, making it one of the more reliable options for on-the-go invoice approval and expense capture. The reconciliation gap remains a challenge for subscription models, as the platform’s matching engine is not optimized for complex, multi-invoice deposits. FreshBooks handles project-based invoicing for agencies and consultancies that send one-off invoices to a small client base. Time tracking integration means billable hours flow directly into invoices without spreadsheet exports or manual entry. If your workflow involves international payroll or complex tax compliance, FreshBooks won’t cover the gap, it’s built for service businesses that invoice on delivery rather than recurring billing models. Price Is No Longer the Barrier With entry-level pricing competitive across the industry, affordability is no longer the primary differentiator. The decision point has shifted to the operational gaps that emerge after adoption, specifically, how each platform handles cash application when deposits arrive without standard references. The same pattern repeats across businesses that outgrow these tools: the finance team starts manually reconciling deposits, late payments start accumulating because no one caught the partial payment, and the AR aging report stops reflecting reality. At that point, the cost isn’t the monthly subscription fee. It’s the unmatched deposits sitting in your bank account while invoices stay open in your system. Where the Category Falls Short None of these platforms fully solve the subscription renewal cash-application bottleneck because they all rely on clean invoice references. When customers use custom reference codes or pay through intermediary processors that strip metadata, manual reconciliation becomes inevitable regardless of which standard tool you choose. The right alternative depends on whether your constraint is AP workflow complexity, choose BILL, regional tax automation and mobile access, choose Zoho Books, or project-based time-to-invoice workflows, choose FreshBooks. If your constraint is recurring revenue reconciliation, all three will force manual work back into your workflow at scale. The decision comes down to understanding which bottleneck you’re solving for before you commit to a platform. FAQ Q: Can BILL.com handle multi-currency transactions for international clients? BILL.com supports multi-currency payments, but its cash application engine still requires exact invoice number references. If an international client pays multiple invoices in one wire transfer or uses a custom reference code, you’ll face the same manual reconciliation bottleneck as domestic transactions. Q: Does Zoho Books integrate with third-party payment processors like Stripe? Yes, Zoho Books integrates with Stripe and other payment processors. The integration handles payment collection, but when Stripe batch-settles transactions or deducts fees before deposit, you’ll need to manually reconcile the net amount against gross invoice totals. Q: How does FreshBooks compare to QuickBooks for small businesses? FreshBooks prioritizes simplicity and ease of use, which works for freelancers and small service businesses. QuickBooks Online offers more comprehensive financial control, including payroll, inventory management, and multi-entity accounting. If you’re processing recurring subscriptions, neither platform fully automates cash application for bundled payments. Q: What happens when a customer pays multiple invoices with one ACH transfer? Most platforms flag the transaction as an exception. You’ll need to manually allocate the deposit across individual invoices. Platforms built specifically for recurring revenue use fuzzy matching to parse payment metadata and automate allocation. Q: Is there a free alternative to these paid invoicing platforms? Wave offers a free plan with basic invoicing and expense tracking. Zoho Books provides a free tier for businesses under $50,000 annual revenue. Both free options still require manual reconciliation for complex payment scenarios. Q: How important is automated cash application for SaaS companies? Automated cash application becomes a scaling bottleneck once you’re processing hundreds of recurring payments monthly. Manual reconciliation delays revenue recognition, creates accounting errors, and consumes finance team capacity that could be spent on growth analysis. Q: Can I migrate from BILL.com to another platform without losing data? Most platforms support CSV exports for customer data, invoices, and transaction history. The migration process typically involves exporting your data, mapping fields to the new system, and importing records. Historical reconciliation may require manual cleanup depending on how the new platform structures its ledger.

title: Voice Typing for Customer Support: Faster, More Human Ticket Replies
summary: How support agents can dictate faster ticket replies with a five-step workflow, privacy notes, and accuracy limits, keeping their own wording instead of AI drafting it.
body_text: Does VoiceOS write my customer support replies for me? No. Dictation Mode only turns your spoken words into text; depending on your Polishing setting it can clean up filler words, punctuation, and (on the 'Polished' tier) awkward phrasing, but it does not generate the reply's content or wording. That's the core difference from an AI-drafting tool, which composes the reply itself from the ticket. [5] Will voice typing work inside Zendesk, Intercom, Freshdesk, or Gmail? Yes. Dictation Mode works in any app or browser field with a text cursor, so it works in whatever helpdesk or inbox a team already uses without a separate integration to set up. [5] How much faster is speaking a reply than typing one? Conversational speech runs about 120-150 words per minute versus roughly 35-65 words per minute for typical keyboard typing, a gap of roughly 3-4x. Those are general population averages, not a measurement of support-ticket replies specifically, so treat it as a directional advantage rather than a guaranteed number for any one queue. [2] [1] Is a dictated reply "AI-written," and can AI detectors tell the difference? No, and this guide doesn't make a claim either way about AI-detection tools; that's not something we've tested or measured. What actually differs is upstream of detectability: with Dictation Mode, the agent decides every word by speaking it themselves, and the software only transcribes (and, depending on Polishing, lightly cleans up) that speech. An AI-drafting tool decides the wording itself from the ticket, and the agent reviews it after the fact. Those are two different authorship processes, whether or not any tool could tell them apart afterward. [5] Is it safe to dictate replies that include a customer's billing or account details? By default, VoiceOS does not use your raw audio, transcripts, or edited text to train its models, and that content is deleted immediately after the processing needed to produce your text, unless you've turned on the optional 'Help Improve VoiceOS' setting, which retains it for evaluation. Producing the transcript does require sending your audio to a speech-processing provider, encrypted in transit and at rest. That's VoiceOS's documented handling, not a substitute for your own company's policy on where customer information can be spoken aloud. [6] [7] What if I don't want VoiceOS changing my wording at all? Set Polishing to 'None' on the Dictation tab for a raw, word-for-word transcript. The default 'Light' setting removes filler words and false starts and fixes punctuation without changing your phrasing; only the 'Polished' tier smooths awkward phrasing. [5]

title: How to Hire Hourly Workers Who Actually Show Up
summary: A practical guide to hiring hourly workers, from where to post and how to screen to closing the gap between an accepted offer and a worked first shift.
body_text: Count an hourly hire only after the person works a first shift. By that measure, most hourly funnels lose more candidates than their owners realize: people skip interviews they scheduled themselves, accept offers and never appear, and read a week of silence as a rejection. In 2025, 41% of organizations facing recruiting difficulty reported a rise in candidate ghosting, with health care and social assistance among the hardest hit. For any operation staffing hourly roles at volume, track interview show rate and response time at every location. The workflow runs from sourcing channels to Day 1 logistics. Judge every stage against one question: does it produce someone who shows up? What hiring hourly workers actually involves Hiring hourly frontline workers is the work of recruiting, screening, scheduling, and onboarding wage-based employees in quick-service restaurants, retail stores, warehouses, delivery fleets, hospitals, and outsourced service operations. In 2025, about 81.5 million U.S. workers were paid hourly rates, and the industries above run on them. At that scale, even local funnel leakage is an operations problem, not just a recruiting metric. The first completed shift is the finish line. An hourly candidate who accepts an offer may still be deciding, because they are often applying to several jobs at once. Everything below assumes the candidate keeps weighing other offers right up until they work that shift. Where hourly candidates come from Hourly sourcing sorts into five channels. Compare them by reach, commute fit, schedule fit, and first-shift conversion, not raw volume: Aggregators and general job boards deliver the widest reach and the weakest signal. Use them for volume, and build the screening to handle everyone they send. Hourly and shift-specific platforms trade pool size for fit. Candidates there already expect wage work and set shifts, so schedule mismatches surface before anyone enters the funnel. Local and community channels punch above their weight for geo-dense roles. Community groups, school partnerships, and transit-adjacent ads reach people for whom a long commute, a common reason hourly workers quit, is less of a dealbreaker than it is on a general board. Referrals and rehire pools carry the highest intent and are the least systematized. A standing referral program prioritizes candidates who already know the job, the manager, and the commute, which heads off week-one surprises. Your own careers page is the only always-on channel you own. It routes candidates straight into your process instead of renting reach from a third-party board. Channel choice sets the ceiling on show-up rate before anyone applies, because a local referral behaves nothing like a candidate who mass-applied from an aggregator at 3 p.m. Compare each source by its last-30-day application-to-first-shift conversion, and move spend toward the channels that produce worked shifts. Writing a job post that pre-qualifies An hourly job post should pre-qualify candidates by stating the pay range, the specific shift pattern, and the street-level location up front. Most advice stops at pay. All three let a candidate self-screen, and that filtering is what protects show rate: among organizations that list pay ranges , 70% reported more applicants and 66% reported higher applicant quality. Shift specificity does the same work in the other direction. A posting that says “flexible schedule” attracts the person who needs Tuesday mornings and the person who needs Saturday nights, and one of them disappears when the real schedule lands. Naming the shift lets a candidate catch the conflict at minute one instead of week two. Rewrite one live posting so the difference is visible: 📢 READY TO BUILD TRUST INTO YOUR HIRING PROCESS? Faster decisions. Fairer outcomes. AI hiring built for compliance, speed, and scale. Leading employers use trust-first AI to: ✅ Reduce bias and improve hiring equity ✅ Automate compliance with built-in safeguards ✅ Increase candidate engagement and completion rates Curious how ethical AI can improve your frontline hiring? 👉 Get Your Personalized Demo Before: “Team Member Wanted. We’re a growing company that values hard work and a positive attitude. We offer competitive pay, a fun team environment, and opportunities for advancement. Candidates should be flexible, reliable, and passionate about customer service. Duties may vary based on business needs. Submit a resume and cover letter to be considered.” After: “Line Cook, $17 to $19 per hour. Friday through Sunday, 11 a.m. to 7 p.m., at 1420 Market Street, near the 12th Street station. Apply from your phone in under five minutes. No resume needed.” The rewrite is shorter because it swaps adjectives for facts a candidate can self-screen against. Screening and scheduling without losing the candidate Most hourly funnels leak at the application and the calendar, so start there. Design the application for a phone, because long, desktop-era forms lose candidates who are applying on a break rather than at a desk. Completion holds up when the form takes about five minutes and drops sharply once it asks 50 or more questions, so cut one hourly application down to a five-minute mobile form with no resume and no account creation. Screen on the three things that actually predict a worked shift: whether the posted shift fits the candidate’s week, whether they have reliable transportation, and whether they can start on Day 1. Schedule fit in particular shows up later in the turnover record. Turnover in the Harvard Shift Project panel of hourly retail and food-service workers ran 39% for people with less than 72 hours of schedule notice versus 24% with two weeks’ notice. Skip the personality and culture-fit questions that predict little at volume, and spend the candidate’s five minutes confirming logistics. Then fold scheduling into screening. Every hour between a completed application and a booked interview gives a competing employer more time to move, and phone tag burns the window while the candidate is still interested. Self-scheduling with multiple time slots lets a qualified candidate book the interview at 11 p.m. from the couch, the moment they applied, instead of waiting for a callback that may never connect. Keeping candidates warm between apply and interview Hourly candidates apply to several employers the same afternoon and commit to whoever stays in contact, so silence is a common reason they slip away. Slow hiring frustrates 57% of frontline candidates, per Fountain’s 2025 Frontline Report, and if you go quiet, another employer contacts and hires them first. Acknowledge the application on arrival, remind the candidate 24 hours and two hours before the interview, and send an update whenever the process pauses. Agentic screening can qualify a new application within minutes, self-scheduling books the interview, and automated follow-up re-engages anyone who stalls, so a candidate usually hears from you before a week of silence reads as rejection. The reminders and screening run automatically; recruiters still approve every disqualification and offer. Fountain’s published MAPS Logistics case study , a UK courier hiring about 2,000 drivers a year, reports a 70% decrease in candidate no-shows alongside automated scheduling with calendar integration plus automated text and email reminders. Test the same scheduling and reminders against your own no-show baseline before assuming the problem is candidate quality. Closing the offer-to-first-shift gap The offer-to-first-shift stretch is the least-managed part of the funnel, where a hire is technically won and still doesn’t arrive. In one survey, about 1 in 5 job seekers accepted an offer and never showed up on Day 1. Assign a recruiter or manager to every accepted offer until the worker completes a first shift, and start pre-onboarding the moment the offer is accepted, so paperwork gets done on a phone that evening and the manager reaches out before Day 1. Send arrival instructions that name the entrance, the on-site contact, and what to wear, and use the early paperwork to surface a new hire’s questions while they are still weighing other offers. Stitch Fix , a warehouse hiring operation that defines its headline metric as applicant conversion, saw the share of applicants who pass background checks and show up on Day 1 rise from 68% to 95%. Measured that way, conversion runs through background checks and Day 1 attendance, which tells you exactly where to remove paperwork and communication friction. Measuring where people disappear Show rate belongs on the leadership dashboard next to time-to-hire and cost-per-hire, as one of the hourly-hiring metrics that predict retention rather than a number a single recruiter tracks. Baseline two figures by location: the share of scheduled candidates who attend the interview, and the share of accepted offers that become a worked first shift. Stage-by-stage conversion shows where the leak sits. Interview-stage drop-off deserves its own location-level measurement, and drop-off by device exposes mobile friction once you compare phone and desktop abandonment. Run the measurement past Day 1, too, so first-shift no-shows and week-two quits stay separate, visible outcomes rather than one blurred number. Frontline new-hire attrition reaches 43% within the first 90 days, so track show rate through the first month, not just to the offer. How Fountain runs hourly hiring end to end Every stage above has to run daily across every location, and manual follow-up breaks first when volume spikes. Cue is the orchestration layer that runs it instead. A regional operator can type a plain-language objective, something like “show me where candidates dropped off between offer and first shift last month, by location, and flag anyone stalled on paperwork,” and get the diagnosis plus the follow-up actions, with a recruiter approving anything sensitive. Underneath Cue, three live agents carry the repetitive work. First, there’s Anna , who handles screening and voice interviews around the clock, so a candidate who applies at 11 p.m. can interview then. Then, Emma , who answers candidate questions at any hour and walks new hires through I-9 and W-4 paperwork, the exact stall point in the offer-to-first-shift gap. Finally, Sam , who monitors post-hire engagement signals past Day 1, where first-shift no-shows and week-two quits hide. The agents run on products that map to the funnel: the ATS for a five-minute mobile application, Onboarding for paperwork closed the evening of the offer, and scheduling and sourcing tools that hold the stages between. Fountain is purpose-built for frontline hourly roles, not a corporate applicant tracking system retrofitted for them, which is why the workflow runs past offer acceptance instead of stopping there. The hire you counted is the one who worked the shift. Book a demo to see Cue, Anna, and pre-Day-1 onboarding run against your own show rate, location by location. Frequently asked questions How do you hire hourly workers quickly? A fast hourly process posts pay and shift details up front, keeps the application under five minutes on mobile, screens on logistics rather than culture fit, lets candidates self-schedule their interview, and contacts applicants the same day they apply. What causes hourly worker no-shows and ghosting? Candidates usually apply to several jobs at once, so slow processes and silence between stages let a competing employer move first. Pay or schedule mismatches discovered late in the process push candidates toward that other offer, which is why stating both up front and staying in contact matter so much. What should an hourly job posting include? Pay range, the specific shift pattern, the exact street-level location, and a mobile apply path that needs no resume, all stated plainly enough that a mismatched candidate self-selects out before booking an interview.

title: What is Value Selling? Techniques and Benefits Explained
summary: Discover value selling techniques and frameworks for B2B SaaS. Learn how to boost close rates, differentiate from competitors, and drive revenue growth.
body_text: Feature-heavy pitching doesn't just fall flat with informed buyers. It signals that the rep hasn't bothered to understand their world. Value selling flips this: instead of leading with what your product does, you lead with what it means for the buyer's business. This post covers everything B2B sales teams need to practice value selling effectively — the definition, a practical three-step framework, five core techniques, and the measurable benefits backed by research. Key Takeaways Value selling focuses on measurable business outcomes — cost savings, time savings, competitive advantage — not product features Winning requires deep buyer research, collaborative ROI development, and proof points tailored to each prospect Top techniques: consultative questioning, ROI quantification, stakeholder-specific messaging, and proof-backed pitching Organizations using value-based selling achieve 52% average win rates vs. 45% for those that don't, per RAIN Group Interactive demos make value tangible before the close — letting buyers experience outcomes firsthand What Is Value Selling? Value selling is a B2B sales methodology where reps shift their focus from product features and specs to the tangible business outcomes a solution delivers. That means leading with cost savings, time recovered, and risk reduction — not "our platform has 200 integrations." The rep's role changes too. Rather than acting like a vendor pitching a product, they position themselves as a consultant who understands the prospect's world: their KPIs, their pressures, and what "success" actually looks like for them. The Four Value Categories That Drive Purchase Decisions Every purchase decision ultimately comes down to one of four things a buyer believes your solution will do for them: Make them more money — revenue growth, new market access, faster sales cycles Give them a competitive edge — capabilities their competitors lack Save them money — reduced headcount, lower operational costs, fewer errors Stabilize and de-risk operations — compliance, reliability, security, continuity ‍ Effective value sellers identify which of these resonates most for each specific prospect — and build every conversation around it. Value Selling in Practice: A B2B SaaS Example Here's the difference in action. A sales rep selling reporting software could say: "Our platform automates report generation with 50+ templates." That's a feature pitch. A value seller says: "Your team is spending roughly 10 hours per week on manual reporting. At your billing rates, that's approximately $4,000 in recovered capacity per month — and your data accuracy problem disappears with it." Same product, completely different conversation — and the second rep wins more deals. That shift in framing has measurable impact. Campminder saw this play out directly. By using Storylane interactive demos as pre-call material, their sales team let prospects self-educate before ever speaking to a rep. The outcome: deals that previously took up to six weeks closed in as little as two weeks — a two-thirds reduction in sales cycle time. The demos shifted the first conversation from basic discovery to high-intent discussion about business fit. Value Selling vs. Consultative Selling These two are often conflated. Consultative selling focuses on asking good questions and diagnosing needs — it's the discovery phase. Value selling goes further by attaching hard financial or operational proof to every recommendation. In practice: consultative selling surfaces the problem, while value selling quantifies why solving it is worth the investment. Why Value Selling Matters in B2B SaaS Today Gartner's data shows that a majority of B2B buyers now prefer to minimize rep involvement in their buying journey. When they do engage with a rep, they expect the conversation to justify the time. That expectation has raised the floor for what "good" looks like in sales — and feature pitches no longer clear it. The High-Growth Adoption Gap Research from ValueSelling Associates and Training Industry found that 87% of high-growth companies use a value-based approach to sales , compared to just 45% of negative-growth companies . The 42-point gap makes a clear case: how you sell is directly tied to whether you grow. Value selling is no longer a differentiator. It's becoming the baseline expectation among high-performing sales organizations. Teams still leading with feature lists are giving ground to competitors who can show measurable business impact from the first conversation. Why Deals Stall Without a Value Case That alignment problem shows up directly in the data. A Forrester survey of more than 18,000 business buyers found 89% had experienced a purchase stall — most often because internal stakeholders couldn't agree on whether the investment was justified. This is where value selling provides a structural advantage. When a rep builds the ROI case collaboratively with the buyer throughout the sales cycle , the buyer can already articulate the business justification internally. The deal doesn't stall at procurement because the financial argument has already been made — by the buyer themselves. Value Selling vs. Solution Selling These two approaches get conflated often — but they operate on fundamentally different logic. Dimension Solution Selling Value Selling Focus Features that solve pain points Business outcomes the solution enables Buyer relationship Vendor-client Advisor-stakeholder Pitch structure Product-led Outcome-led Negotiation dynamic Feature comparisons, discount pressure ROI already established, less price sensitivity Deal quality Transactional, higher churn risk Strategic, stronger retention ‍ ‍ Solution selling works by identifying a pain point and showing which product features address it. The problem, as HBR noted , is that modern buyers now define their own solutions — which turns sales conversations into feature-comparison exercises and pushes suppliers toward price-driven bake-offs. Value selling avoids that trap. By the time negotiations start, the ROI case has been built collaboratively with the buyer. When they've helped calculate the return, there's little incentive to push for discounts. How to Build a Value Selling Framework Value selling is a repeatable process, not a personality trait. This three-step framework gives reps a structure they can apply deal by deal. Step 1: Research and Understand Buyer Needs Thorough preparation before any pitch is non-negotiable. Before the first call, reps should review: The prospect's LinkedIn profile and recent activity Company website, recent press releases, and earnings reports (if public) Competitor landscape and known industry pressures CRM history for any prior interactions The goal isn't just industry knowledge. It's understanding the specific role's KPIs, what success looks like for that person , and where the most acute pressure points are. Discovery calls in value selling are structured differently than standard demos . The priority is helping the prospect quantify their own problem — not pitching. Open-ended questions like "What does this problem cost you in time or revenue each month?" surface the pain in the buyer's own language. Follow-ups help them paint a picture of the cost of inaction before a single feature is mentioned. Step 2: Map Pain Points to Value Drivers Once the pain is surfaced, break it down into specific problems and map each one to a value driver: Manual data updates → Time saved + accuracy improved High error rates in reporting → Cost reduced + risk mitigated Slow competitive response time → Competitive edge gained Then build the ROI case. The key is doing this with the buyer, not presenting it to them. Use data from existing customer outcomes as benchmarks, but let the prospect validate the numbers against their own context. Gartner research found buyers are 1.8x more likely to complete a high-quality deal when they use supplier-provided digital tools in partnership with a sales rep — collaborative value development, not one-sided persuasion. Forrester backs this from the buyer side: 97% of B2B enterprise buyers build a business case before making a purchase, and 41% specifically want ROI and business-impact data from vendors. The business case isn't optional — it's expected. Step 3: Deliver a Tailored, Proof-Backed Pitch That ROI case becomes the backbone of your pitch. Structure it in three parts: Confirm their problem — restate the pain in their language, showing you listened Map the solution to outcomes — connect specific product capabilities to the value drivers you identified Prove it with a relevant story — use a customer case study that mirrors the prospect's situation ‍ Story selling matters here. Abstract claims about "efficiency gains" don't resonate. A specific story about a similar company solving a similar problem — with a measurable result attached — does. Interactive demos extend this further. Rather than describing the value, let the prospect feel it. Storylane's buyer hubs let reps consolidate demos, case studies, ROI resources, and collateral into a single personalized link for each account. Reps can segment content by stakeholder role — a CFO view focused on ROI, an end-user view showing workflow impact — and track which sections each stakeholder engages with most. When a champion needs to sell internally, they have everything they need in one place. Demo tokens allow reps to personalize demos with the prospect's company name, industry-specific data, and relevant use cases in seconds — no manual rebuilding per account. Respond.io used this approach and saw a 162% increase in trial clicks and a 2x increase in engagement by structuring their demos around specific value propositions . Key Value Selling Techniques and Best Practices Technique 1: Be a Consultant, Not a Salesperson The mindset shift is from "how do I sell this?" to "how do I help this person solve their problem?" Prospects respond to being understood, not pressured. Avoid rushing to the pitch — use early interactions to gather information and build credibility. Rushing the pitch signals that the rep cares more about quota than outcomes. That destroys trust before value has a chance to land. Technique 2: Bring Fresh Insights to Every Interaction Top-performing sales reps are 33% more likely to inspire buyers with new ideas and perspectives than average performers, according to RAIN Group research across 700+ B2B purchases. In practice, this means arriving at every touchpoint with something new: a relevant data point, a customer story, an insight specific to their industry. Tools like Storylane's account reveal show exactly which features a prospect spent the most time exploring, so reps can lead the next conversation with those specific capabilities rather than recycling a generic pitch. Technique 3: Quantify Value in the Buyer's Language Abstract claims don't close deals. Specific numbers do. Train reps to translate every benefit into financial or operational impact: "Saves time" → "Saves your team 8 hours per week, which at your billing rate is approximately $X per month" "Reduces errors" → "Eliminates the rework cost you estimated at $Y per quarter" "Speeds up reporting" → "Gets your team from first draft to final report in 2 hours instead of 2 days" Use existing customer metrics as benchmarks. Demo analytics — tracking time spent on specific features, return visits, and completion rates — give reps concrete benchmarks to show prospects where others in similar roles focus their attention. Technique 4: Tailor Your Message to Each Stakeholder Value means different things to different people in a buying committee. Effective value sellers adapt their message to the role, not just the company — a pitch that resonates with an operations leader will bore a CFO. Stakeholder What They Actually Care About CFO Cost savings, ROI, payback period End user Time saved, ease of use, reduced frustration CTO Risk mitigation, integration, security, scalability Operations leader Process efficiency, error reduction, compliance ‍ ‍ Storylane's buyer hubs support this by organizing content paths by persona — each stakeholder sees the version of the value story most relevant to their priorities. Technique 5: Pace the Conversation to the Buyer's Readiness Don't jump to ROI before the buyer has fully articulated their problem. If a prospect is still in early research mode, pushing a financial case creates misalignment. Provide resources that help them define their needs first : audits, checklists, use case demos. Once a prospect moves into active evaluation, timing matters. Storylane's intent scoring classifies demo engagement as low, medium, or high based on time spent, completion rate, features explored, and return visits. Reps get Slack alerts when high-intent accounts engage, so outreach hits at moments of genuine buyer interest rather than cold guessing. Benefits of Value Selling for B2B Sales Teams Higher Win Rates and Growth Correlation The performance gap is measurable. RAIN Group data shows value-driving sales organizations achieve a 52% average win rate , compared to 45% for non-value-driven organizations . That seven-point gap compounds across a full pipeline. At the organizational level, 87% of high-growth companies use value-based selling vs. 45% of negative-growth companies. The methodology doesn't guarantee growth, but high-growth teams have adopted it at a far higher rate. ‍ Better Deal Quality and Margin Protection When the ROI case is built collaboratively before negotiation, buyers have less reason to push for price concessions — they've already done the math on the return. The negotiation shifts from "can we lower the price?" to "when can we get started?" Storylane's internal data supports this: prospects who engage with interactive demos before sales conversations convert at 3.2x the rate of those who don't (10.1% vs. 3.1%). A buyer who has experienced the product before the close negotiates from understanding, not skepticism. Stronger Long-Term Customer Relationships Value selling doesn't end at the signed contract. Reps who follow up post-sale to confirm that promised outcomes were actually delivered create the conditions for renewals, expansions, and referrals. Dreamdata used Storylane interactive demos for expansion conversations, with 17% of upsell revenue influenced by the platform. Their approach — letting champions share demos with executives who don't have time to explore the product themselves — made the expansion value case easy to communicate internally without requiring another live demo. When buyers have internalized the value at every stage — not just at close — renewals and expansions become a natural next step rather than another sales conversation. Frequently Asked Questions What is the meaning of value selling? Value selling is a sales methodology where reps focus on demonstrating measurable business outcomes — cost savings, time savings, competitive advantage — rather than product features. The rep acts as a consultant who connects their solution to the specific results the prospect is trying to achieve. What is an example of value-based selling? Instead of saying "our platform has automated reporting," a value seller says: "Our platform eliminates 5 hours of manual reporting per week — for your team size, that's roughly $2,000 in recovered productivity per month. The error rate drops to near zero, too. Same product, entirely different conversation. What is the difference between value selling and solution selling? Solution selling matches product features to pain points. Value selling connects the solution to measurable business impact. Value selling typically produces less price sensitivity at negotiation because the ROI case is built collaboratively with the buyer before the deal closes. How do you quantify value for a prospect? Work with the buyer to calculate ROI using their own numbers — time spent, headcount, current costs — combined with benchmarks from existing customers. The more the buyer helps build the estimate, the more they trust it. How long does a value selling sales cycle typically take? Value selling cycles tend to run longer than transactional approaches because each interaction is built around delivering insight and building a shared ROI case. The trade-off is deal quality: higher close rates, less discounting, and lower post-sale churn.

body_text: View All News Letter to Surf Air Mobility Inc. Shareholders from Chairman of the Board August 3, 2026 LOS ANGELES--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- The following is a letter to Surf Air Mobility Inc. shareholders from Shawn Pelsinger, Chairman of the Board: I am honored and excited to take on the role of Chairman of the Board of Surf Air Mobility. In my decade at Palantir, where I served as the Global Head of Corporate Development, I witnessed firsthand what the right software can do to accelerate an industry in transition. Air mobility is at that moment right now, and I believe Surf Air Mobility is perfectly positioned to capture the opportunity. In late 2024 we laid out our Transformation Plan. We set out to improve our capital structure, optimize our operations, and incubate our SurfOS business. As I write to you today, we have significantly reduced our debt, improved profitability in our air mobility business, and we have secured our first multi-million-dollar contract to deploy SurfOS alongside Palantir. The Transformation Plan was designed to get our house in order, because we knew that without a stable foundation we could not deliver consistent and timely execution against our biggest opportunities. I believe that we have executed our plan successfully, and we now have the foundation that allows us to move into a new chapter for the company. We had to raise and invest capital over the last several years to build a technology-enabled platform that can grow both revenue and profitability simultaneously. We now intend to prove it to you. Our singular mission has never changed: to transform air mobility. What has evolved over the years is how best to approach that massive market opportunity. To lay it out plainly, this is how we see our business today: SurfOS: An AI-enabled operating system built with Palantir, serving enterprise and small and medium sized clients across the industry, that generates high-margin software revenue and deploys next-generation technology the industry needs for its next growth phase. Tech-enabled charter platform: A platform that aligns operators, owners, brokers, and passengers, so that every stakeholder who deploys the software grows the value of the entire ecosystem. Air mobility operations: A profitable air mobility operation to be the commercial launchpad for next-generation electric aircraft. Let me give you a little more detail on what the next chapter of Surf Air Mobility looks like and how our three interconnected parts of the business translate into long-term economic value. Our next chapter makes SurfOS air mobility’s digital infrastructure. We built an AI-enabled operating system with Palantir and proved it inside our two airline brands and a fast-growing charter business. We are now commercializing this software. Few companies sit where we sit, at the intersection of aviation operations, AI-enabled software, and electrification, and we intend to use our position to our advantage. During the initial deployment of any emerging software platform, early enterprise contracts are often short-term and modest in value, but we intentionally set a high bar for ourselves. Winning Wheels Up as our first enterprise software customer, worth up to $12 million over the contract term, is not a “typical” first deal. It is a multi-year, multi-million-dollar contract that shows you our ambition paid off. It also tells you that the product is working and the market is ready. And this customer is deploying just one product within our growing platform. OperatorOS, OwnerOS, and OEM OS are yet to launch commercially. Our enterprise pipeline is growing and we have the weight of Palantir behind our go-to-market. We have barely scratched the surface. Our next chapter proves our platform strategy through our charter business. Our private charter business will be our largest growth engine and is the anchor of our platform strategy. Through our charter business, we currently interface with the brokers, operators, owners, manufacturers, and passengers that comprise the value chain. Today, the private charter value chain is fragmented and misaligned. Aircraft owners, brokers, and operators use dozens of disconnected, inefficient systems. By organizing them through SurfOS, our platform can create efficiencies and margin expansion that only occur when incentives are aligned. As more stakeholders increasingly come on platform, the results will show up in more revenue and in expanding margins, not just for us, but for others as well. In other words, we expect our Surf On Demand private charter business to keep growing, and we expect the platform to grow even faster. Like platform businesses that have transformed other industries, our goal is to help organize the supply and demand through our technology to create a distributed air mobility network that gets more reliable, efficient, and profitable over time. Our next chapter turns our airline into the launchpad for electric flight. At present, we are not interested in chasing topline airline revenue for its own sake. Instead, we see our operational footprint, especially in Hawaii, as a technology proving ground and as the place to bring new electric aircraft into commercial use. Our ambition is to be the first airline to fly a paying passenger on an electric aircraft. When BETA's aircraft are certified to fly commercially, Hawaii is where they will fly first, on routes we already operate, with AI-enabled software already running the operations. You'll see the airline become a smaller share of the business, while becoming more cash generative, and when paired with technology from partners like BETA and our own SurfOS software, our airline operations will inflect even further to profitability. Where our focus is for the rest of this year and into 2027. To sum it up, here is the shortlist of what we are working toward through the back half of this year and throughout 2027: Rolling out SurfOS products for enterprise and small to medium size customers Establishing a path to profitability in each of our businesses Significantly growing charter platform revenue Flying the first paying passenger on an electric aircraft once certified My primary duties as Chairman are simple: allocate capital wisely and ensure our team executes with relentless discipline. I'm excited to take this journey with you. Shawn Pelsinger Chairman of the Board Surf Air Mobility About Surf Air Mobility Surf Air Mobility is a Los Angeles-based air mobility platform. With its AI-enabled SurfOS software, Surf Air Mobility provides technology designed to support the modernization of air operations and the adoption of next-generation aircraft. The Company currently operates one of the largest commuter airlines in the United States by scheduled departures and provides private charter services. Together, these businesses provide the operational scale and real-world operating data to validate and deploy its software. These capabilities position Surf Air Mobility as a leader shaping a more efficient, connected, and accessible future for aviation. Forward-Looking Statements This letter contains forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995 — including statements about our Transformation Plan and path to profitability in each business, the commercialization and expected benefits of SurfOS, growth of our charter platform (including our target of charter platform revenue above $100 million), and the timing and commercial deployment of electric aircraft with BETA. These reflect management's current views and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially, including: our limited operating history and the fact that we have not yet commercialized OperatorOS, OwnerOS, or OEM OS for third-party sales; development delays, technical challenges, or lack of market acceptance affecting the return on our SurfOS investment; our dependence on Palantir, BETA, and other partners and suppliers; the timing of regulatory certification of electric aircraft and any accidents or incidents involving them; our customers' ability to pay for our services; our ability to fund operations, satisfy our obligations, and access financing on acceptable terms; our continued compliance with New York Stock Exchange listing standards; and general economic conditions. These and other risks are described in the periodic reports we file with the SEC (available at www.sec.gov ), which you should review before making an investment decision. We assume no obligation to update these statements except as required by law. Surf Air Mobility Media Contacts Press: press@surfair.com Investors: investors@surfair.com Source: Surf Air Mobility Inc.
