title: 11 Best SaaS Web Design Agencies in 2026
summary: Compare the 11 best SaaS web design agencies in 2026 by operating model, with published pricing, accessibility guidance and honest fit notes.
body_text: Key takeaways: A SaaS website has to match the product it sells, so the agency you hire needs to design marketing pages and product UI without the two drifting apart. Published rates run from $1,490 a month on a subscription to $11,999 a month for two dedicated designers, and most of the category still quotes privately. Since 28 June 2025 the European Accessibility Act has applied to e-commerce services, while WebAIM found detectable accessibility failures on 95.9% of the top million home pages. Pick by operating model first: a dedicated designer, an unlimited queue, a scoped project or a growth retainer are four genuinely different purchases. Most website advice assumes you sell something a visitor already understands. SaaS doesn't work that way. You're asking someone to grasp an abstract product from a screenshot, trust you with their data, and start a trial before anyone has spoken to them. That puts unusual weight on a handful of pages, and it means your marketing site and your product interface are judged as one thing. A slick homepage in front of a dated dashboard reads as a bait and switch. This list covers the SaaS web design agencies worth your shortlist in 2026, sorted by the operating model they actually sell rather than by a star rating. We're first, and we've said plainly which jobs the others do better. If you'd rather bring the work in-house, the same criteria apply when you hire a SaaS designer directly. Why SaaS websites are a different design problem Three constraints separate SaaS web design from ordinary web design. The first is that you have two interfaces. The marketing site sells the promise and the product delivers it, and when their visual languages diverge, activation suffers. Agencies that only do marketing sites hand you a beautiful front door attached to someone else's house. The second is that the site never stabilizes. You ship features continuously, so pages need adding and rewriting every few weeks, which is a poor fit for an agency that works in three-month scoped projects and then disappears. The third is that the pricing page carries more revenue weight than anything else on the site, and it is genuinely hard to design. It has to express tiers, usage limits, seat math and an upgrade path without making a prospect feel trapped. Any agency you shortlist should be able to talk fluently about all three. If the conversation stays on visual style, you're talking to a studio that will treat your SaaS product like a brochure, which is the difference between a marketing vendor and a genuine SaaS design service . The 11 best SaaS web design agencies The table sorts by operating model, because that decides more about your experience than portfolio quality does. Published prices appear where a firm actually publishes them, and "quote only" is the honest answer everywhere else. Agency Operating model Best for Published pricing Location Awesomic Subscription, unlimited queue Marketing site plus product UI, brand and video from one team $1,490 to $2,995 a month Remote, San Francisco Eleken Dedicated designer, monthly SaaS product UI where one designer learns your app deeply $4,599 to $11,999 a month Ukraine, serving US and EU Wavespace Project and retainer Framer and Webflow sites for funded startups Quote only Global CodeTheorem Project SaaS founders building AI features into the product Quote only India, serving global clients Arounda Project and team extension Brand, website and product design as one holistic system Quote only Ukraine, serving US and EU SimpleTiger Retainer SaaS sites where organic search is the growth channel Quote only Sarasota, Florida Koombea Project Web apps and platform work alongside the marketing site Quote only United States and Latin America Flowout Subscription and hourly packages Enterprise Webflow builds with predictable scope From $5,900 to $9,900 a month Remote, Europe-based Pony Studio Project and ongoing support SaaS brands that need identity and interface together Quote only London, plus four other cities Grafit Agency Project Conversion-focused component builds on a deadline Quote only Poland, serving global clients Market8 Retainer, limited slots Early SaaS founders wanting positioning before pixels Quote only Doral, Florida The pattern worth noticing is that only three of eleven publish a number, and those three all sell recurring models. Project agencies price on discovery, so expect a call before a figure. 1. Awesomic Best for: SaaS teams whose website and product both need design attention, without hiring for each. The two-interface problem is the one we're built for. The same matched designer can take your pricing page on Monday and a settings screen on Thursday, which is how the marketing site and the product stay recognizably the same product. You send work to a queue instead of scoping a new engagement each time. That suits how SaaS actually ships. Feature launches arrive with a landing page, a changelog entry, an in-app announcement and a deck, and those are four different disciplines that usually mean four different vendors. Core services: SaaS marketing sites and landing pages, product UI/UX, Webflow and Framer builds, brand identity, pitch decks, video and motion, copywriting and QA on All-in-One. How it works: Describe the job, from a pricing page rebuild to an ongoing design queue. A vetted designer suited to that work picks it up, typically inside a day. Review in Slack and request unlimited revisions. Keep adding tasks as the roadmap moves, with no per-task pricing. Pricing: Graphic Pack sits at $1,490 a month and All-in-One at $2,995, with quarterly billing taking 20% off either. Dedicated Talent pairs a full-time talent with a PM and is priced on request. Honest limits: we're a design subscription, not a growth retainer, so we won't run your paid acquisition or own your SEO strategy the way SimpleTiger or Market8 will. What we can show is range on real SaaS work. For Mercoa, which sells embedded bill payments to B2B fintech platforms through a single API, we handled UI/UX design and the Webflow build together. Want to see whether the model fits your roadmap? Get started . 2. Eleken Best for: SaaS companies whose product UI is the bottleneck, not the marketing site. Eleken describes itself as a pragmatic UI/UX agency for SaaS, and its pitch is turning clunky MVPs and developer-designed tools into usable products. You get one dedicated designer working your queue, with a Head of Design overseeing quality rather than a project manager relaying messages. Core services: SaaS product UI/UX, product redesign, design from scratch, team extension, design systems. Pricing: published and unusually specific. $4,599 a month for a part-time designer, $6,599 for a full-time designer, $11,999 for two. Two-month minimum, three-day free trial, pause or cancel anytime. Its real strength: depth on one product. A designer who spends months inside your app makes better decisions than one who visits it quarterly. The tradeoff is scope, because this is product UI/UX only, with no branding, video or marketing collateral in the package. 3. Wavespace Best for: funded startups that want design and front-end build from a single team. Wavespace positions as a global UI/UX agency for startups and enterprises, building websites and apps in Framer and Webflow with design and development under one roof. Its homepage claims work with companies backed by Y Combinator, a16z, Sequoia and Techstars, and says more than 550 founders have used it. Core services: UI/UX design, Framer and Webflow development, brand, product design. Pricing: nothing public; a number follows the scoping call. Why buyers shortlist it: the single-team model removes the handoff gap where a design gets approved and then quietly gets worse during build. Treat the investor logos as an indication of the market it serves rather than a quality guarantee. 4. CodeTheorem Best for: SaaS teams adding AI capability and needing the interface to make it legible. CodeTheorem pairs UI/UX design with custom development, and its stated focus is helping founders design and build AI-powered products ready for growth. That combination is genuinely useful right now, because most SaaS products are bolting AI features onto interfaces designed before those features existed. Core services: UI/UX design, custom software and AI development, product design for SaaS founders and product teams. Pricing: unpublished. Where it fits: best when the design question and the engineering question are the same question. If you only need a marketing site refresh, this is more capability than the job needs. 5. Arounda Best for: SaaS companies that want brand, website and product treated as one system. Arounda describes itself as a design and development studio uniting brand identity, web development and UI/UX into a single product, and it has worked with recognized brands and Fortune 500 companies alongside startups. The holistic framing is the point: it's aimed at teams tired of a logo from one vendor, a site from another and an app from a third. Core services: brand identity, UI/UX design, web development, product design, team extension. Pricing: nothing public, and the estimate tracks how many surfaces you need. What it's genuinely good at: consistency across surfaces, which is the exact failure mode SaaS companies hit when they grow through separate vendors. 6. SimpleTiger Best for: SaaS companies where organic search is the primary acquisition channel. SimpleTiger is a B2B SaaS marketing agency, and web design sits inside a practice built around search. Webflow is its build platform of choice, and the argument for hiring it is that the site architecture, the content model and the keyword strategy get decided together instead of in sequence. Core services: SaaS SEO, web design and Webflow development, paid search, content. Pricing: unpublished, and sold as a retainer rather than a one-off build. Why it earns a place here: redesigns are the most common way SaaS companies accidentally destroy their organic traffic, and a team that owns both sides has an obvious incentive not to. Be clear that you are buying a marketing retainer with design inside it, not a design studio. 7. Koombea Best for: SaaS products where the web app itself needs building, not just the site around it. Koombea is a software development firm with dedicated web app design, web development and website redesign practices, and it holds Clutch Premier Verified status. It runs project-based and team-extension engagement models, so it can take a defined build or embed alongside your engineers. Core services: web and mobile app development, web app design, website redesign, product strategy. Pricing: nothing public. Estimates come out of its own scoping process. Where it beats the alternatives: when the hard part is the application rather than the pages selling it. For a pure marketing-site refresh, the lighter teams on this list will move faster. 8. Flowout Best for: SaaS marketing teams that want Webflow work at a fixed monthly rate. Flowout sells unlimited Webflow design and development on a subscription, and it holds Webflow Premium Partner status at the enterprise tier. Plans stack by scope rather than by seat, and it also sells SEO, conversion rate optimization and blocks of hours for teams with irregular demand. Core services: Webflow development, UX/UI design, custom development and interactions, conversion-focused copywriting, project management. Pricing: published. From $5,900 a month for development, $7,900 with design, and $9,900 with design and copywriting, on monthly, quarterly or yearly billing. Hourly packages come in 25, 50 and 100-hour blocks. Why buyers shortlist it: the pricing is genuinely transparent for this category, and the hourly blocks are a sensible way to keep a Webflow specialist available without a full retainer. It is Webflow-only, so it is not the team to ask about platform choice. 9. Pony Studio Best for: SaaS companies whose brand needs to catch up with the product. Pony calls itself the branding agency for emerging tech, working out of London and across New York, San Francisco, Amsterdam and Berlin. It runs three connected practices: brand strategy and identity, interfaces spanning websites through to native and web apps, and ongoing creative support for marketing teams. That last one matters for SaaS, where demand after launch is steady rather than occasional. Core services: brand strategy, visual identity and logo, website and app interfaces, decks and campaigns, ongoing creative support. Pricing: unpublished. Its real strength: identity work that carries through into product screens rather than stopping at a brand book. If your visual identity is already settled and you only need pages built, you would be paying for strategy you don't need. 10. Grafit Agency Best for: tech companies that want a conversion-focused rebuild inside a tight window. Grafit sells growth-driven design across design, development and growth, and it leads with outcomes rather than aesthetics. Its featured case study is a component-based build for Callstack delivered in six weeks that it reports lifted conversions by 176%. Core services: web design, component-based development, conversion optimization, growth support. Pricing: nothing public, though it does post current availability. What to know before hiring: the component-based approach is the useful detail, because it leaves your marketing team able to assemble new pages without going back to the agency. Treat the 176% figure as one project's reported result rather than a benchmark. 11. Market8 Best for: early-stage SaaS founders who need positioning resolved before design starts. Market8 works with a deliberately small number of SaaS companies at a time and frames its offer around growth strategy and B2B web design together. It says outright that it does not think of itself as an agency, which reads as positioning but does describe the engagement: fewer clients, more strategic involvement. Core services: SaaS growth strategy, positioning and messaging, B2B web design, demand generation. Pricing: unpublished. Where it fits: valuable if your real problem is that nobody can explain what you do in a sentence, since no amount of design fixes that. Less relevant if your messaging is settled and you need execution volume. How we vetted this list We pulled every agency named across the current search results for SaaS web design, then cut the list down with four tests. The first was whether the agency exists. Four firms named in live 2026 SaaS roundups could not have taken the work. BX Studio, listed at number six in one current article, is now a parked domain, and Spot On Agency is openly for sale at $299. MakeBuild and FlowTrix do not resolve at all. Open every link in every list, this one included. The second was whether the agency actually serves SaaS. One widely cited roundup lists Barrel as a top SaaS web design agency; Barrel's own homepage describes it as a CPG commerce agency working with Shopify DTC brands. Good agency, wrong list. The third was whether web design is a real service rather than a keyword. We dropped several B2B marketing agencies whose sites never mention design work, and kept SimpleTiger and Market8 because both name it as a service and we've flagged the retainer context in their entries. The fourth was usefulness at different budgets and stages, so the list spans a $1,490 subscription and a $11,999 two-designer engagement rather than eleven versions of the same offer. The four pages that decide whether a SaaS site converts Most SaaS redesigns spread effort evenly across thirty pages. Traffic and revenue do not distribute that way, and a good agency will push back on an even split. Homepage: name the category, the buyer and the outcome above the fold, then show the product interface rather than an abstract illustration. Pricing: publish real numbers wherever you can, define what a seat or a credit means, and make the upgrade path visible. Product or feature pages: one job per page, with a screenshot of the actual screen and the specific limitation it removes. Signup or demo: strip every field you do not need on day one, and make clear what happens next. Ask any agency to walk you through how it would handle those four before you discuss visual direction. The answers separate teams that understand SaaS from teams that build attractive sites, and they surface fast whether the agency has ever designed a web app interface as well as pages about one. The failure modes here are consistent enough to be predictable. A developer offering free teardowns on Reddit , off the back of a decade building SaaS marketing sites, told one founder he had to read the whole page and watch the demo before working out the product was even a web app, then found the hero's "Get Started" button dropped him on a login screen. That's one reviewer's opinion rather than research, but both faults are cheap to check on your own site this afternoon. Accessibility stopped being optional in 2025 This is the change most SaaS teams have not priced in. The European Accessibility Act, Directive 2019/882 , has applied since 28 June 2025 to services provided to consumers in the EU, and e-commerce is explicitly named in its scope. If you sell subscriptions into Europe, the accessibility of your purchase flow is now a legal question rather than a design preference. The gap between that requirement and the state of the web is enormous. The 2026 WebAIM Million analysis of the top one million home pages found detectable WCAG 2 failures on 95.9% of them, up from 94.8% the year before, at an average of 56.1 errors per page. The failures are mundane rather than exotic. Low contrast text appeared on 83.9% of pages, missing image alternative text on 53.1%, and missing form input labels on 51%, and that last one lands squarely on your signup form. Practically, ask a prospective agency two questions: what contrast standard they design to, and whether they test forms with a keyboard and a screen reader before handing over. An agency that treats this as a developer's problem at the end of the build will leave you with the errors above. What SaaS web design actually costs Published rates are rare, so anchor on the three firms here that do publish and treat everything else as a starting point for negotiation. Model Typical cost What you're buying Best when Unlimited design subscription $1,490 and $2,995 a month Queued requests across site, product and brand Demand is constant and varied Dedicated designer $4,599 to $11,999 a month One or two designers embedded in your product Product UI is the bottleneck Webflow subscription $5,900 to $9,900 a month Ongoing Webflow build, design and copy at a fixed rate You are committed to Webflow Scoped project $20,000 to $120,000 A defined redesign with discovery, design and build A launch or rebrand with a finish line Growth retainer $8,000 to $20,000+ a month Web design inside SEO, content and demand generation Marketing is outsourced end to end Only the first three rows come from published prices. The project and retainer ranges describe how these firms characterize their engagements rather than rates they publish, so confirm before you plan around them. The more useful comparison is against the alternative of hiring. One mid-level product designer costs a full salary and covers one discipline, which is why the freelancers versus agencies versus subscriptions question usually resolves on breadth rather than headline rate. Agency, subscription, or in-house? Three models, three different failure modes. A scoped project agency gives you senior strategic attention and a defined outcome, and it leaves. That's correct for a rebrand or a funding-round refresh, and wrong when the site needs weekly attention, which is when teams start queueing changes for a redesign that never comes. A subscription gives you continuous capacity and no scoping overhead, and it works when the volume of small work is high. It's the weaker choice when you need a named strategist running research workshops with your executive team. An in-house designer gives you the deepest product context of any option, and caps out at one person's skill set. Most SaaS companies discover this when the designer who is excellent at product UI is asked to cut a launch video, which is the gap outsourced product design usually fills alongside a hire rather than instead of one. The mistake to avoid is picking a model to match your budget and then being surprised by how it behaves. Match it to the shape of your demand instead, then find the best firm inside that model. Running your shortlist Take three agencies, not eight. Give each the same brief, with your actual traffic numbers and the specific pages you think underperform, and ask what they would change first and why. Two answers tell you most of what you need. Ask what they would do about your pricing page, since it exposes whether they understand SaaS economics or just layout. Then ask who maintains the site ninety days after launch, because the honest answers split neatly between the project firms and the recurring ones, and the design agency checklist we use covers the rest of the diligence. If your answer is that the site and the product both need steady attention and you would rather not hire twice, that's the case for a subscription, and it's the case we make for ourselves. If you need one deep, senior engagement with a clear finish line, several firms above will serve you better than we will, and we'd rather say so than win the wrong project. FAQs Do I need a SaaS web design agency or a product design agency? A SaaS web design agency builds the marketing site that turns a visitor into a trial or a demo. A product design agency designs the application itself. Several firms here cross that line deliberately, including Eleken on the product side and Arounda across both, but most specialize. Decide which surface is your bottleneck before you brief anyone, because the strongest marketing-site agency may have never designed a dashboard. How much does a SaaS website redesign cost? It depends entirely on the model. Subscriptions start at $1,490 a month, dedicated-designer arrangements run $4,599 to $11,999 a month, and Webflow-focused subscriptions sit between $5,900 and $9,900. Scoped project rebuilds commonly land between $20,000 and $120,000 depending on page count and integrations. Only a minority of agencies publish rates, so expect a discovery call before a number. Does my SaaS website need to meet accessibility standards? If you sell to consumers in the EU, the European Accessibility Act has applied since 28 June 2025 and names e-commerce in its scope, so your purchase flow is covered. Beyond compliance, the common failures are things that hurt every user, and WebAIM found missing form input labels on 51% of the top million home pages, which directly affects signup completion. Should we use Webflow or a custom build for a SaaS site? Webflow suits most SaaS marketing sites because it lets marketing publish without a developer, which matters when you ship features monthly, and it is the platform behind much of our own Webflow work. A custom build earns its cost when you need deep application integration, unusual performance requirements, or content structures Webflow's CMS cannot model. Be aware that Webflow-only agencies will always recommend Webflow, so ask a platform-neutral team if the choice is genuinely open. How long does a SaaS website project take? A scoped redesign typically runs two to four months: discovery and messaging, then design, then build and QA. Grafit publishes a six-week component-based build as a featured case study, which is fast and depends on decisions being made quickly. Subscriptions work differently, shipping a page at a time from within a day or two of starting, which suits teams that would rather improve continuously than relaunch.

title: Quality, Innovation, and High-Value Care at Home
summary: Adoration Home Health delivers skilled, compassionate care in the home for patients recovering after acute illness, managing chronic conditions, or
body_text: Quality, Innovation, and High-Value Care at Home August 12, 2026 Adoration Home Health delivers skilled, compassionate care in the home for patients recovering after acute illness, managing chronic conditions, or needing rehabilitation to restore strength, mobility, balance, endurance, self-care, and independence. Services also include medication reconciliation, patient and caregiver education, and care coordination. As part of BrightSpring Health Services, Adoration combines local home health teams with broader home and community-based infrastructure across home health and hospice, with private duty services available in select markets.[1-5] 2026 quality results demonstrate an operating model focused on timely access, functional recovery, patient experience, documentation discipline, and branch-level accountability. Home health reached 98.9% timely initiation of care (97.4% SHP national average), 86.1% discharge function (78.6% national), 86.5% patient satisfaction (81.0% national), and 93.2% of branches rated at least four stars (90% internal target).[6] The same quality infrastructure also spurs areas of innovation. A continual focus and programming centered on disease-state management and reducing potentially preventable hospitalizations are embedded throughout the organization. Other ongoing initiatives include branch-level performance-improvement projects, after-hours triage, chart audits, OASIS documentation improvement, and education designed to identify clinical deterioration early while preserving appropriate escalation when a patient’s condition requires it. [6,15] Innovation strengthens this clinical model. BrightSpring’s Vitality Therapy™ program brings a structured anti-frailty intervention into the home health episode, translating evidence on strength, gait speed, balance, independence, and frailty into a practical care pathway for older adults recovering at home. [7] Scale and infrastructure support consistency. BrightSpring adds enterprise-level quality systems, clinical support capabilities, pharmacy and medication-management assets, workforce development, and data-driven operating disciplines that help local Adoration teams respond reliably to patient and referral-partner needs. [8-10] Two BrightSpring family-of-brands integrations further differentiate Adoration from a stand-alone home health agency. Abode Care Partners provides home-based primary care for older adults and complex populations, while Continue CareRx adds pharmacy-enabled medication reconciliation, adherence packaging, synchronized home delivery, pharmacist review, virtual nursing support, and 24/7 medication access. Together, these capabilities address two common drivers of avoidable utilization after discharge – gaps in longitudinal primary care and medication-management failure – and help knit home health into a broader home-centered platform. title: Sismo en tu conjunto: qué hacer y a quién acudir
summary: Qué hacer si un sismo afecta tu conjunto residencial: quién responde primero, cómo se clasifica el daño y a qué autoridades acudir en Colombia y Panamá.
body_text: El 10 de agosto de 2026, un sismo de magnitud 7.4 con epicentro en San José del Palmar, Chocó, sacudió buena parte de Colombia y se sintió con fuerza en ciudades tan lejanas como Bogotá, Cali y Manizales, además de percibirse en Panamá, Ecuador y Venezuela. Las consecuencias fueron graves: edificaciones colapsadas, cientos de personas fallecidas y miles de damnificados. Es un recordatorio doloroso de algo que muchas administraciones de propiedad horizontal no tienen del todo claro: qué hacer, en las horas inmediatas, cuando un sismo afecta tu conjunto o edificio. Este artículo no pretende sustituir ninguna orientación oficial de las autoridades de gestión del riesgo. Su objetivo es ayudarte a entender la cadena de respuesta —quién actúa primero, quién decide qué y a quién acudir según lo que necesites— para que, si el momento llega, tu comunidad sepa exactamente qué hacer. La cadena de respuesta: quién hace qué en las primeras horas El guardia de seguridad: primera línea de contención. Inmediatamente después de que cesa el movimiento, el guardia de turno es quien tiene el primer contacto con la situación real del conjunto. Su función no es evaluar daños estructurales —eso corresponde a un profesional— sino activar el protocolo interno de emergencia del PH: verificar que las rutas de evacuación estén despejadas, apoyar la salida ordenada de residentes si así lo determina el plan de emergencias, y reportar de inmediato al administrador cualquier situación visible de riesgo (grietas evidentes, elementos desprendidos, olor a gas). El administrador: coordinación y comunicación oficial. Una vez recibido el reporte del guardia, el administrador tiene tres responsabilidades inmediatas: activar el plan de emergencias de la copropiedad, contactar a un ingeniero civil con experiencia en patología estructural para una evaluación técnica si hay señales de daño, y comunicar a todos los residentes, de forma oficial y centralizada, el estado del edificio y los pasos a seguir. Esta comunicación es crítica: en medio de una emergencia, la desinformación y los rumores se propagan más rápido que cualquier instrucción oficial. Las autoridades técnicas: quiénes evalúan si el edificio es seguro. Ni el guardia ni el administrador —por más experiencia que tengan— están habilitados para determinar si una edificación es segura para habitarse después de un sismo. Esa evaluación corresponde a un ingeniero civil, idealmente con especialidad en patología de estructuras, o a los equipos técnicos de la entidad distrital o municipal de gestión del riesgo (como el IDIGER en Bogotá, u organismos equivalentes en otras ciudades), que aplican metodologías estandarizadas de inspección post-sismo. Cómo se clasifica el daño de una edificación Las guías técnicas de inspección post-sismo utilizadas en Colombia clasifican una edificación en uno de cuatro niveles, con base en criterios objetivos —continuidad de columnas y vigas, inclinaciones, desplazamientos, grietas en elementos estructurales— y no en una impresión visual aislada: Habitable: sin daños que comprometan la seguridad estructural. Uso restringido: puede usarse parcialmente, con limitaciones específicas mientras se realizan reparaciones. No habitable: no debe ocuparse hasta que se resuelvan los daños identificados. Peligro de colapso: riesgo inminente; debe evacuarse y acordonarse de inmediato. Es importante entenderlo: no todas las grietas significan daño estructural grave, pero tampoco corresponde a un residente o administrador decidir eso por su cuenta. Ante cualquier duda, lo correcto es no ingresar y solicitar la evaluación profesional. A quién acudir según el tipo de ayuda que necesitas Rescate o emergencia médica inmediata: línea de emergencias 123 en Colombia; en Panamá, el Sistema Nacional de Protección Civil (SINAPROC). Evaluación estructural del edificio: un ingeniero civil matriculado con experiencia en estructuras, o la entidad distrital/municipal de gestión del riesgo de tu ciudad. Reporte de daños y coordinación institucional: la Unidad Nacional para la Gestión del Riesgo de Desastres (UNGRD) en Colombia, o SINAPROC en Panamá. Cobertura de daños patrimoniales: tu aseguradora, con quien debes reportar el siniestro tan pronto como sea posible, idealmente con fotografías del daño. El rol de la comunicación digital en medio de la emergencia En un momento así, lo último que necesita una comunidad es depender de cadenas de WhatsApp fragmentadas o rumores sin confirmar. El módulo de Avisos y Comunicados de Munily permite al administrador enviar una actualización oficial a todos los residentes al mismo tiempo —estado del edificio, punto de encuentro, próximos pasos— con la certeza de que llega a cada unidad y queda registrada en el historial de la app, en lugar de perderse entre mensajes sueltos. Para situaciones individuales —un residente que necesita ayuda dentro del conjunto tras el sismo, por ejemplo si quedó atrapado en un área común o necesita asistencia inmediata del guardia— el Botón de Pánico permite notificar directamente al equipo de seguridad con un solo toque desde la app, dejando un registro trazable de cómo se atendió la situación. Ninguna de estas herramientas sustituye a los organismos de socorro ni a la evaluación de un ingeniero estructural: su función es que la comunidad se mantenga coordinada e informada mientras esos procesos avanzan. Ningún protocolo elimina el miedo o la incertidumbre que deja un sismo, pero sí puede evitar que la confusión se sume al daño. Saber quién responde primero, cuándo acudir a un profesional y cómo mantener a tu comunidad informada marca una diferencia real en las horas más difíciles. Si tu comunidad quiere conversar sobre cómo mantener una comunicación clara y centralizada en momentos de emergencia, en Munily estamos para acompañarte.

title: IBM Connects Its First Modular Cryogenic Systems in Milestone Toward Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
summary: The new architecture is designed to scale into the modular, shared, and ultra-cold system required to link hundreds of quantum chips into a more powerful quantum computer capable of solving large problems.
body_text: YORKTOWN HEIGHTS, N.Y., August 19, 2026 — IBM (NYSE: IBM ) today announced it has successfully joined and cooled down two cryogenic modules into a single environment. The new architecture is designed to scale into the modular, shared, and ultra-cold system required to link hundreds of quantum chips into a more powerful quantum computer capable of solving large problems. Its deployment is a milestone on IBM's path to delivering IBM Quantum Starling in 2029, which is expected to be the world's first fault-tolerant quantum computer and will integrate advances across error correction, processor design, decoding, and systems engineering. Combined, the first two operational modules stand more than 8 feet tall and 8 feet wide, and initial tests demonstrated they can jointly cool down to 4 Kelvin (the temperature of liquid helium) in under 5 days, reaching a final temperature of below 15 millikelvin shortly after. Each module’s vacuum enclosure offers up to 12 times more wiring space than the most widely used IBM quantum systems, enabling more chip-to-chip connections both within and between modules. IBM’s new box-shaped design allows modules to connect in a tight row and use this larger space to directly link quantum processors with IBM’s “L-coupler” technology. L-couplers connect separate quantum chips together to share information, communicate, and operate as part of a larger quantum computer. By 2027, IBM’s quantum roadmap plans to use L-couplers to link multiple processors into a larger quantum computer with at least 1,000 programmable qubits, which are qubits that can be directly used to perform computations. Towards this goal, IBM will install IBM Quantum Nighthawk processors into the cryogenic modules later this year to expand operational performance testing. At the time Starling is delivered, IBM plans for each cryogenic module to house thousands of qubits. IBM’s plans for Starling were introduced last year with a new error correction code that dramatically reduces the physical resources required for fault tolerance. Since then, the company’s progression has remained on course , including the demonstration of core hardware components and breakthroughs in efficient error-correction decoding. "Bringing fault-tolerant quantum computers to industries depends on several fundamental advances,” said Jay Gambetta, Director of IBM Research and IBM Fellow . “The successful connection and operation of these cryogenic modules signals a leap forward in that direction and will accelerate our progress alongside continued innovation in quantum hardware, software, and algorithms.” IBM expects its scalable cryogenic modules to help speed its pace of innovation. For example, three essential components of IBM Quantum System Two’s environment are built into the new architecture, but now in a way that allows each part to be independently tested, improved, and rapidly iterated. The delivery of these new cryogenic quantum modules is further evidence that IBM is systematically delivering against its quantum roadmap, solving another one of the major hurdles required to accelerate its path to fault-tolerant quantum computing. About IBM IBM is a leading provider of global hybrid cloud and AI, and consulting expertise. We help clients in more than 175 countries capitalize on insights from their data, streamline business processes, reduce costs and gain the competitive edge in their industries. Thousands of governments and corporate entities in critical infrastructure areas such as financial services, telecommunications and healthcare rely on IBM's hybrid cloud platform and Red Hat OpenShift to affect their digital transformations quickly, efficiently and securely. IBM's breakthrough innovations in AI, quantum computing, industry-specific cloud solutions and consulting deliver open and flexible options to our clients. All of this is backed by IBM's long-standing commitment to trust, transparency, responsibility, inclusivity and service. Visit www.ibm.com for more information. Media contacts: Dave Mosher IBM dave.mosher@ibm.com Erin Angelini IBM edlehr@us.ibm.com

title: Mini PCs Explained: What They’re Good For and Why Shoppers Love Them
summary: Learn what Mini PCs are good for, how they compare with laptops and desktops, and what to check before buying one.
body_text: If you want a real desktop experience without giving up a ton of space, a Mini PC is worth a serious look. These compact systems are popular for home offices, streaming setups, classroom use, and everyday computing because they bring the essentials of a full PC into a much smaller footprint. That small size is only part of the appeal. Mini PCs can also be a smart buy when you want a cleaner desk, lower noise, and a system that can slide into places a tower never would. Here’s a closer look at how people actually use them and why they’ve become such a practical option. 1. Start with the main purpose of a Mini PC The big idea behind a Mini PC is simple: deliver desktop computing in a very compact design. For most buyers, that means getting the everyday performance they need while taking up far less room than a traditional tower. That makes Mini PCs especially appealing for tight spaces like dorm rooms, apartments, shared offices, reception counters, and compact home workstations. Many models can also be mounted behind a monitor with a VESA bracket, which helps keep your setup neat and frees up even more desk space. 2. Understand the most common ways people use them For many shoppers, a Mini PC is the perfect everyday machine. Web browsing, email, video calls, streaming, document editing, and spreadsheet work are all common tasks for these systems. If you want something quiet and unobtrusive for daily use, this form factor makes a lot of sense. Mini PCs also show up in plenty of specialized setups that don’t need a big desktop tower: Home office and remote work Classroom or student setups Media playback and TV streaming Point-of-sale or retail kiosk systems Home labs and small servers Light photo editing and casual content creation 3. Know where a Mini PC makes the most sense Mini PCs shine when you care more about convenience, space savings, and low noise than maximum expandability. They’re a strong match for buyers who mainly use cloud tools, office apps, browsers, and video conferencing software. They’re also a practical choice in spots where a full-size desktop would feel bulky or out of place. Think meeting rooms, store displays, entertainment centers, or shared family spaces. In those situations, the compact footprint is more than a nice bonus; it’s exactly why the system works. 4. Compare Mini PCs with laptops and desktops A Mini PC sits in a very useful middle ground. Compared with a laptop, it can offer a more comfortable desktop setup because you can pair it with the monitor, keyboard, and mouse you actually want. Compared with a tower desktop, it usually takes up far less space and is easier to tuck away. The tradeoff is that Mini PCs usually have less room for upgrades and fewer high-performance options than larger desktops. If your priority is heavy gaming, advanced 3D rendering, or demanding professional workloads, a full-size desktop may still be the better investment. Mini PC: best for compact, quiet, everyday use Laptop: best for mobility Desktop tower: best for performance and expandability 5. What to look for before buying one When you’re shopping for a Mini PC, the key is to focus on what will affect daily use. Size matters, but it’s the processor, memory, storage, and ports that determine how well the system fits your workflow. Here’s a simple checklist to help you shop smarter: Processor: choose a current Intel Core, AMD Ryzen, or similar chip for smoother multitasking. Memory: 8 GB is the minimum for light use, while 16 GB or more is better for multitasking. Storage: an NVMe SSD is strongly preferred for fast boot and app loading. Ports: check for HDMI, DisplayPort, USB-C, and enough USB-A connections. Networking: Wi-Fi and Ethernet are important for stable home and office use. If those specs line up with how you plan to use it, a Mini PC can be one of the most efficient upgrades you make. Summary Mini PCs are popular because they make desktop computing easier to fit into real life. They’re compact, versatile, and well suited for everyday productivity, entertainment, kiosk use, and even light server duties. If you want a capable PC that won’t dominate your desk, this category deserves a spot on your shortlist. Frequently Asked Questions Can a Mini PC handle everyday office work? Yes, a modern Mini PC is usually a strong fit for email, web browsing, document editing, spreadsheets, and video calls. For smoother multitasking, choose a model with a current CPU, 16 GB of RAM, and an NVMe SSD. Is a Mini PC a good value compared with a laptop? It can be a very good value if you already own a monitor, keyboard, and mouse. A Mini PC often gives you a more comfortable desktop-style setup for the money, while a laptop includes portability that you may not need. How much performance can I expect from a Mini PC? Most Mini PCs are best for daily computing, media streaming, office apps, and light creative work. They are not usually the best choice for heavy gaming, advanced 3D rendering, or demanding workstation tasks. What should I check about warranty before buying one? Look at the warranty length, who handles support, and whether accidental damage is covered. It is also worth checking how easy it is to get service, replacement parts, or a swap if something goes wrong. Are Mini PCs usually in stock, and do models change often? Stock and configurations can change quickly because Mini PCs are often refreshed with new processors, RAM, or storage options. If you find one that fits your needs, it is smart to confirm availability and return policies before waiting too long. a Read More ASUS ExpertCenter PB64 — Official ASUS product page for a compact business mini PC with modern Intel processors. title: Principal Financial Well-Being Index | 2026 Wave 2
summary: Understanding employer and employee sentiment through meaningful business research and analysis.
body_text: Principal Financial Well-Being IndexSM 2026 Wave 2 The Principal Financial Well-Being Index is our comprehensive quarterly study of the financial health of U.S. employers. The index score factors in business health, growth, and optimism based on economic outlook. Our research draws insights from business owners, key decision makers, and executive leaders across organizations ranging from small businesses to large enterprises (2–10,000 employees) that offer employee benefits and retirement plans. All businesses Small businesses Large businesses Business financial health Businesses’ perceptions of their own growth have declined after a year of stagnation, falling even lower than their previous three-year low in April 2025. Meanwhile, optimism about the U.S. economic outlook over the next 12 months has also fallen, diverging from how businesses view their own financial growth. These shifts resemble businesses’ reactions to the Liberation Day tariff announcements. 28-pt. gap March 2021 Businesses were struggling through the pandemic but incredibly hopeful. 9-pt. gap March 2026 Businesses’ financials are worse than last year; they appear to be losing hope that things will get better soon. “Employers across all business sizes are now confronting a more uncertain environment after entering the year with confidence in their ability to navigate policy changes and economic volatility. Small businesses are paying close attention to forces beyond their immediate control, changing how they plan. Even local decisions are now informed by global dynamics, pushing employers to focus on efficiency and near-term resilience.” Amy Friedrich President, Benefits and Protection, Principal® Business concerns % responding that the area is a “significant” or “major” concern Table that conveys percent of areas that are a significant or major concern for businesses. Area of concern All employers Cost of healthcare 59% Economic inflation 51%, up from 44% in January 2026 Cost of offering benefits 50% Stability of the U.S. economy 48% Energy and fuel price volatility 48% Potential for a recession 44%, up from 36% in January 2026 “Economic anxiety among U.S. small businesses is rising sharply, with recession risk increasingly front of mind. High interest rates, tariffs, supply chain disruptions, and energy costs are compressing margins and pulling small firms into the same macro pressures long faced by large businesses. What’s shifted is perspective: Owners are now watching geopolitics, shipping lanes, and trade policy, because global shocks are directly shaping local outcomes.” Seema Shah Chief global strategist, Principal Asset Management® Businesses continue to evaluate staffing and benefit strategies Hiring and staffing levels remain largely unchanged since January 2026. The prominent concern is finding qualified workers at a time when changing jobs may be considered risky. As a result, benefits are under closer scrutiny. While cutting benefits could ease short-term budget pressure, many employers recognize they can’t afford to lose top talent—making affordability versus benefit richness the key tradeoff. How businesses are evolving their benefits in 2026 Businesses that are expanding or optimizing benefits are focusing on health insurance, retirement benefits, mental health and well-being, key employee benefits, and voluntary benefits. Those considering cuts are far more selective, with health insurance often the only area adjusted—highlighting how few benefits employers feel they can afford to reduce without risking talent loss. Businesses in active expansion (11%) Health insurance (56%) Retirement benefits (55%) Mental health and well-being (53%) Key employee benefits (45%) Specialized care and family support (43%) Businesses in strategic evaluation and optimization (59%) Health insurance (59%) Retirement benefits (44%) Mental health and well-being (41%) Voluntary/employee-paid benefits (33%) Specialized care and family support (29%) Businesses in strategic consolidation (9%) Health insurance (42%) Financial support (37%) Voluntary/employee-paid benefits (36%) Retirement benefits (35%) Mental health and well-being (29%) “In 2025, businesses anchored their confidence in the strength of their own operations, even amid market volatility. That confidence has been tested this year by higher fuel costs, persistent inflation, and growing recession concerns. Still, many small and midsize businesses continue to look ahead with cautious optimism—focused on protecting what’s in front of them today while preparing for opportunities that lie ahead.” Amy Friedrich President, Benefits and Protection, Principal® 2026 2025 2024 2023 2022 2021 Principal Financial Well-Being Index℠ Wave 1 Principal Financial Well-Being Index℠ Wave 3 Principal Financial Well-Being Index℠ Wave 2 Principal Financial Well-Being Index℠ Wave 1 | Download full report (PDF) Principal Financial Well-Being Index℠ Wave 3 (PDF) Principal Financial Well-Being Index℠ Wave 2 (PDF) Principal Financial Well-Being Index℠ Wave 1 (PDF) Principal Financial Well-Being Index℠ Wave 3 (PDF) Principal Financial Well-Being Index℠ Wave 2 (PDF) Principal Financial Well-Being Index℠ Bank Pulse (PDF) Principal Financial Well-Being Index℠ Wave 1 (PDF) Principal Financial Well-Being Index℠ Wave 3 (PDF) Principal Financial Well-Being Index℠ Wave 2 (PDF) Principal Financial Well-Being Index℠ Wave 1 (PDF) Principal Financial Well-Being Index℠ Wave 3 (PDF) Principal Financial Well-Being Index℠ Wave 2 (PDF) Principal Financial Well-Being Index℠ Wave 1 (PDF) Methodology The Principal Financial Well-Being Index℠ (WBI) Wave 2 (March 13–27, 2026) is recurring research used to track sentiment around repeated financial health measures and timely issues relevant to businesses. Business owner, decision maker, and leader participants who represent companies with 2–10,000 employees (n=1,000) provide information by completing a 15-minute online survey. Access to sample is provided by ROI Rocket, a third-party research panel provider. Some quotes have also been provided by current Principal customers. In 2025, the WBI added a formal index. The index number in the WBI is calculated by taking responses from six perceptual measures evaluating current financial health, financial comparisons year over year, and projections for business and economic outlook. title: Restaurant Demand Forecasting for Delivery Orders
summary: Build a practical delivery-order forecast by store, marketplace, and daypart, then measure the misses and improve it every week.
body_text: Restaurant Demand Forecasting for Delivery Orders Most restaurant forecasts start with one daily sales number. That is usually too blunt for delivery. A location can finish Tuesday close to plan while dinner delivery misses badly. Promotions, outages, and marketplace shifts can distort the baseline and hide the actual workload. This matters because delivery is no longer a side channel. The National Restaurant Association reports that nearly three-quarters of restaurant traffic happens off-premises. Its May 2026 survey also found that, among restaurants offering third-party delivery, 63% of limited-service and 41% of full-service operators are available on three or more platforms. ( National Restaurant Association ; May 2026 survey ) A useful forecast has to reflect demand moving through separate systems. What is restaurant demand forecasting for delivery orders? Restaurant demand forecasting is the process of estimating future orders, sales, and workload from historical patterns plus known factors such as promotions, holidays, weather, and local events. For delivery, the useful forecast is not one restaurant-wide number. It is a forecast by location, marketplace, and daypart that teams can compare with actual results. A forecast is not a target. A target says what the business wants to achieve. A forecast says what is likely to happen under current conditions. If a location’s target is above the clean forecast, the team needs a plan to close the gap. Entering the target into a spreadsheet does not make it demand. For most operators, the best starting unit is: Location x marketplace x daypart x orders Forecast order count first because orders create kitchen workload. Then estimate sales by multiplying expected orders by a realistic average order value for that same channel and daypart. Why should delivery demand be forecast separately? Delivery does not move exactly like dine-in or pickup. Marketplace ranking can change visibility. Promotions can pull demand into one channel. A store can be paused while the dining room remains busy. Cancellations can reduce completed orders without reducing kitchen touches. Weather may push people from dining out to ordering in, but the effect will vary by concept, item, and market. A 2024 restaurant-chain study in the International Journal of Forecasting tested internal and external data with machine-learning and deep-learning models, reinforcing a practical point: data selection matters as much as model choice. ( International Journal of Forecasting ) The goal is not to build the fanciest model. It is to stop feeding obvious distortions into a simple one. Which signals belong in a delivery forecast? Start with signals you can explain and maintain. Clean delivered-order history Use completed orders by location, marketplace, weekday, and daypart. Keep sales and average order value beside order count, but do not let revenue alone drive the forecast. Ten large family orders and 25 single-meal orders can produce similar sales with very different kitchen pressure. Store availability and downtime A period when the store was unexpectedly offline is not normal demand. Mark it as suppressed demand instead of treating the lower order count as a clean baseline. If you are unsure whether a weak period was demand or execution, first diagnose a delivery sales drop . Cancellations and acceptance problems Track placed orders, accepted orders, completed orders, and cancellations separately when the data is available. A spike in canceled orders can signal real customer demand that the operation failed to fulfill. Promotions and advertising Label every historical period that had a promotion or meaningful ad change. Do not compare a discounted Friday with a full-price Friday and call the difference seasonality. Before using a promotion lift as a future adjustment, measure delivery app promotion ROI and determine whether the lift was truly incremental. Calendar and local events Federal and provincial holidays, school breaks, sports, concerts, conventions, paydays, and tourism can shift demand. Keep only the events that have shown a repeatable effect for that location. Weather Weather belongs in the review, but not as a universal multiplier. A 2025 study found weather and daypart useful for predicting hot- and cold-drink sales, but not total sales in that dataset. Test the effect on your own concept. ( PMC ) For Canadian locations, include snow, extreme cold, and tourism patterns. Restaurants Canada’s 2025 trends report also highlights changing affordability and digital-first behavior, so recent local history deserves more weight than a national assumption. ( Restaurants Canada ) How do you build a weekly delivery demand forecast? Use this seven-step process: Choose the forecast unit. Start with completed orders by location, marketplace, and daypart. Pull comparable periods. Compare Tuesdays with Tuesdays, dinner with dinner, and the same channel with itself. Remove distorted periods. Flag downtime, unusual closures, major listing errors, one-off catering orders, and promotion spikes. Calculate a weighted baseline. Give more weight to the most recent clean comparable period. Add known adjustments. Apply local factors for a scheduled promotion, holiday, event, weather pattern, or operating-hours change. Publish three scenarios. Give teams a floor, likely case, and high-demand case. Compare actuals and record the reason for the miss. The explanation is what improves next week’s forecast. Run the process on the same day every week. A forecast that is updated casually will become another spreadsheet nobody trusts. What simple forecasting formula can a restaurant use? An independent operator can start with a weighted moving average: Baseline forecast = (last comparable period x 50%) + (two periods ago x 30%) + (three periods ago x 20%) Example: a restaurant is forecasting Friday dinner delivery orders for one marketplace. Last clean Friday: 118 orders Two Fridays ago: 110 orders Three Fridays ago: 104 orders The baseline is: (118 x 0.50) + (110 x 0.30) + (104 x 0.20) = 112.8 orders Round the likely case to 113 orders. Now assume the restaurant has a promotion scheduled. Its own past results show that the same promotion produced an 8% incremental order lift at this location after removing orders that likely would have happened anyway. Adjusted likely forecast = 113 x 1.08 = 122 orders That 8% is a local planning assumption, not an industry benchmark. Without reliable history, keep the baseline and widen the scenario range. For example: Floor: 110 orders Likely: 122 orders High: 134 orders How should the forecast change staffing and prep? Do not hand the kitchen only a sales number. Translate the forecast into orders, items, and arrival windows. If one order averages 2.4 items, 122 forecast orders represent roughly 293 items, but the item mix still determines prep, cook, packaging, and handoff load. Use the likely scenario for the core plan: Prep quantities for the expected item mix. Labor coverage for the busiest 30- or 60-minute window. Packaging and label supply. A pickup-area capacity check. A backup action if volume reaches the high case. The high scenario should trigger a specific response, such as opening a second packing position or moving a cross-trained employee to expo. For known event spikes, pair the forecast with the playbook to prepare for peak delivery demand . How do you know whether the forecast is improving? Track forecast accuracy at the same level where the decision was made. If the team forecast Friday dinner by store and marketplace, do not score the result using total weekly brand sales. A good location can hide a bad location in the roll-up. Two metrics are enough to start. Weighted absolute percentage error WAPE = total absolute forecast error / total actual orders x 100 If four locations forecast 500 total orders and the combined absolute error is 60 orders, WAPE is 12%. Lower is better, but there is no universal “good” percentage. Set a baseline and improve against your own history. Forecast bias Bias = (total forecast orders - total actual orders) / total actual orders x 100 Positive bias means the team consistently over-forecast. Negative bias means it under-forecast. WAPE tells you how far off the forecast was. Bias tells you which direction the misses lean. Add one reason code to every material miss: Promotion performed differently Store downtime Weather effect Event effect Listing or menu issue Staffing or acceptance constraint Unexplained After several weeks, those notes often matter more than another layer of math. How should multi-unit teams scale the process? Use one forecasting language across the brand, then let local evidence change assumptions. Corporate or regional teams should define: The forecast unit and daypart boundaries. Which order statuses count. How downtime and cancellations are treated. Which promotions require a separate baseline. The scenario format. The accuracy metrics and review cadence. Store managers should own local adjustments for events, road closures, campus calendars, weather, and unusual operating conditions. Every override needs a reason. A practical cadence is: Monday: central team publishes the baseline. Tuesday: stores add approved local adjustments. Wednesday: regional leaders review large exceptions. Daily: actuals replace assumptions and major misses receive a reason code. Monthly: the team reviews WAPE, bias, and recurring root causes by location. That turns forecasting into a management process instead of a spreadsheet exercise. Which forecasting mistakes create false confidence? Blending every channel: Keep dine-in, pickup, first-party delivery, and each major marketplace separate until the operating plan is built. Treating downtime as low demand: If customers could not order, replace that period with a clean comparable baseline. Copying promotion lift across stores: Use local evidence, not the portfolio average. Forecasting dollars but staffing orders: Kitchen workload follows tickets, items, and arrival concentration. Using one exact number: Publish floor, likely, and high cases. Ignoring the reason for a miss: Without a reason code, the same error returns next week. How can Voosh support a cleaner delivery forecast? Forecasting depends on a reliable historical picture. That becomes harder when sales, cancellations, promotions, reviews, and store availability live in separate marketplace portals. Voosh helps connected restaurant teams review delivery sales, mix, cancellations, and marketplace performance by store, channel, and daypart. Depending on enabled modules, teams can also examine store uptime, reviews, and ads or promotions. VooshGPT can help operators investigate what changed and why actual demand differed from plan. That makes Voosh useful at two points: Before the forecast: build a cleaner marketplace baseline. After the forecast: investigate the variance instead of labeling every miss “demand.” Voosh does not replace a POS, inventory platform, labor scheduler, weather feed, or marketplace setup process. It provides a more connected view of delivery signals. For the broader reporting foundation, see the restaurant dashboard for delivery operators . Turn forecasting into a weekly operating habit Restaurant demand forecasting does not need to start with AI. Begin with a clean unit of analysis, three comparable periods, transparent adjustments, and a weekly accuracy review. The big shift is simple: stop forecasting the restaurant as one number. Forecast the location, marketplace, and daypart that will create the work. When the baseline is clean and every miss has a reason, the forecast becomes more useful each week. Prep gets tighter and teams spend less time reacting. Want to see how Voosh connects delivery performance across stores and marketplaces? Book a demo .

title: Three Beasley Leaders Earn National Recognition
summary: NAPLES, FL — August 17th, 2026 — Beasley Media Group is proud to celebrate three outstanding programming leaders who have earned national recognition for
body_text: NAPLES, FL — August 17 th , 2026 — Beasley Media Group is proud to celebrate three outstanding programming leaders who have earned national recognition for their dedication, innovation and commitment to local radio. Rick Radzik, Program Director of WBZ in Boston; Chuck Damico, Program Director of WMMR, WXTU and WMGK in Philadelphia; and Jade Springart, Director of Rock Programming for WRIF and WCSX in Detroit, have been named to Radio Ink’s 2026 list of “Radio’s Most Successful Program Directors.” The honor recognizes the leadership these talented professionals bring to their stations, teams and communities every day. RICK RADZIK Beasley Media Group Program Director Boston, MA WBZ In Boston, Radzik continues to demonstrate the power of live, local radio. Whether WBZ is reacting instantly to breaking sports news or bringing listeners, staff and sponsors together to support Special Olympics Massachusetts, he understands that people and community remain at the heart of the medium. “We could not have done all that without humans,” Radzik said while reflecting on WBZ’s ability to quickly mobilize its team for hours of live coverage following a major Celtics trade. CHUCK DAMICO Beasley Media Group Program Director Philadelphia, PA WMMR/WXTU/WMGK In Philadelphia, Damico leads three iconic brands while embracing the expanding opportunities available across audio, video, social media and other platforms. “The mission every day is to make a sincere emotional connection with the listener,” Damico said. He also credited his teams for continuing to produce top-tier programming and effective marketing campaigns despite a rapidly evolving media landscape. JADE SPRINGART Beasley Media Group Director of Rock Programming Detroit, MI WRIF/WCSX Springart brings that same commitment to Detroit, where WRIF and WCSX remain deeply connected to their audiences through local personalities, music, sports and community-focused content. While she sees opportunities to use emerging technology as a creative tool, Springart believes authentic human connections remain essential. “I firmly believe our stations thrive…on our personalities and our listeners relating to a real person talking to them,” she said. At the heart of Rick, Chuck and Jade’s work is a genuine belief in what makes local radio so special: the power of human connection. They all bring that belief to their own station’s, creating meaningful relationships with listeners, supporting their teams and making a difference in their communities. We are grateful for their work that truly represents the very best of Beasley Media Group and demonstrates the enduring impact of great local radio. Congratulations to Rick, Chuck and Jade on this well-deserved recognition! READ THE FULL ARTICLE at RadioInk.com

Most families hit hit a moment when they realize that the home that made sense when they moved in just isn’t big enough anymore for their growing family. Kids outgrow sharing a room and want their own spaces. The kitchen no longer comfortably holds everyone invited to mealtimes. And constantly moving furniture around, hoping that’ll create a little more space – never quite does. OR, perhaps a single person decides they want more space with options for an office or future possibilities. Or a couple wanting a little extra room for just about anything. The Banner line of homes offers: An affordable step up with modern, durable finishes and features built for family life or for a future-ready individual Well-designed, flexible floor plans in single and multi-section options to support your goals Quality Cavco construction at family-friendly, affordable prices Shop our Banner Line of homes here What Makes a Cavco Banner Home Family Friendly? A home from the Cavco Banner line is for the family or individual ready for the next chapter, offering extra features and options and room to grow. A little more space, with the details that make daily life easier and extra comfortable. Homes in the Banner line feature: Generous kitchen islands with room to prep, have coffee, work from home, do homework — all the activities that make the kitchen the center of life Modern, durable finishes that look sharp on day one and hold up through years of real life – the meals, pets, projects, kids and everything in between Ample storage throughout with smart designs to help a busy household stay organized now and into the future Flexible living spaces designed to adapt as routines change and needs shift over time Choice of family-friendly layouts with single and multi-section floor plans to match an individual’s, couple’s or family’s size, space and living needs Built by Cavco – a nationally recognized manufactured home builder with more than 60 years of experience building quality, high-value, affordable homes for families and individuals from coast to coast and in parts of Canada These well-considered details and features – a properly sized kitchen, a comfortable layout, finishes that last – add up to a home that lives and feels right every day. Find Your Banner Floor Plan How Are Banner Homes by Cavco Built? Banner homes are built the way all Cavco manufactured and modular homes are – inside a climate-controlled facility, to the strict standards of the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) called the HUD Code , then transported to customer’s home site and professionally installed. Building indoors means construction never stops for weather. Materials stay protected throughout the entire build. And because Cavco purchases materials in large quantities, the savings get passed along to buyers in the form of more affordable home prices. Every home in the Banner home line meets national standards for structural integrity, energy efficiency, fire resistance, plumbing and electrical systems – and is verified by independent third-party inspectors before it ever leaves the facility. The Vantage Banner series double-section home. 3 bedrooms | 2 baths | 1680 sq. ft. 30′ x 56′ How Much Does a Banner Home Cost? Homes in the Banner home line are at one of our most affordable price points to give growing families more space and family-friendly features – without putting a Banner home out of reach. The easiest way to get a hard price is to start by shopping online in your area and then contacting your local home dealer . Pricing varies by floor plan, location and what’s included in the retailer’s turnkey quote. Most Cavco retailers build their quotes to cover the home, delivery within a set distance, placement on the foundation and basic site preparation – so you know what you’re getting without having to worry about hidden costs at the end. Your local retailer can walk you through an itemized quote that fits your specific situation. It also helps to know that manufactured homes typically cost up to 30% less than comparable onsite-built construction – a savings gap that comes from a more efficient build process, bulk materials purchasing and no weather delays. Where Can I Buy a Home from the Cavco Banner Home Line? Homes in the Banner home line are sold through company-owned and independently owned Cavco retailers nationwide – and finding a Cavco retailer near you takes under a minute. It's really quick and easy – Use Cavco's Find Your Home tool to enter your ZIP code and browse available homes in the Banner home line at local retailers, complete with photos, floor plans, video walkthroughs and contact information. Land – Many Cavco retailers connect buyers with local real estate professionals who specialize in finding land for manufactured homes or may have retailer-owned lots available in your area. Move-in-ready homes – Some locations have Banner homes already placed and ready for you to purchase and move in. Find A Local Cavco Home Dealer Is Buying a Home from the Banner Home Line a Smart Long-Term Investment? Do Banner homes appreciate in value ? A Banner home line house builds equity the same way any home does – through location and consistent maintenance, not construction method. Homes built off site generally appreciate at the same rate as other similarly maintained homes built on site in the same area. What matters is where the home sits and how well it’s cared for – not whether it was built in a factory or framed on a lot. For growing families, there’s also the straightforward math of monthly costs. A home from the Banner home line typically offers more predictable payments than renting a house with comparable space. And instead of building someone else’s equity with every rent check, you’re building your own equity and a heritage to leave to your family. Room to Live. Space to Grow. Kids have outgrown sharing a room and need their own space, life has gotten bigger and the home you started in has stopped keeping up. Room to cook. Room to gather. Finishes that hold up to real family life. And a price that means comfort doesn't have to come at the expense of financial peace of mind. Because a home should grow with you. Homes in the Banner home line by Cavco were built to make sure it can. Find a Banner home near you and connect with a local Cavco retailer to get started. Banner Homes Frequently Asked Questions Who are Banner homes designed for? Homes in the Banner home line are designed for growing families and busy households that need room to grow and space to live and want to stay within a realistic budget. Your local Cavco retailer can walk you through what’s available in your area. Do I need to own land to buy a home from the Banner home line? Not necessarily. Ask your local retailer what’s available near you. Are Cavco homes energy efficient? Yes. Are Banner homes well-built manufactured homes? Banner homes are HUD Code manufactured homes, built in a climate-controlled facility, transported to your home site and professionally installed.
